𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory and contractible varieties: a survey

Aravind Asok    Paul Arne Østvær
Abstract

We survey some topics in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory. Our main goal is to highlight the interplay between 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory and affine algebraic geometry, focusing on the varieties that are “contractible” from various standpoints.

1 Introduction: topological and algebro-geometric motivations

In this note, we want to survey the theory of varieties that are “weakly contractible” from the standpoint of the Morel–Voevodsky 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory of algebraic varieties. The current version of this document is based on lectures given by the first author at the Fields Institute workshop entitled “Group actions, generalized cohomology theories and affine algebraic geometry” at the University of Ottawa in 2011, and the Nelder Fellow Lecture Series by the second author in connection with the research school “Homotopy Theory and Arithmetic Geometry: Motivic and Diophantine Aspects” at Imperial College London in 2018.

As a source of inspiration, we review some aspects of the theory of open contractible manifolds, which has source in one of the first false proofs of the Poincaré conjecture, and served as a testing ground for many ideas of classical geometric topology in the 1950s and 60s. We also review some aspects of the theory of complex algebraic varieties whose associated complex manifolds are contractible. Along the way we formulate some problems that we feel are interesting.

1.1 Open contractible manifolds

Suppose MnM^{n} is an nn-dimensional manifold, which we take to mean either topological, piecewise-linear (PL) or smooth (we will specify). Say an nn-manifold MnM^{n} is open if it is non-compact and without boundary. As usual, let II be the unit interval [0,1][0,1]. Recall that MnM^{n} is called contractible if it is homotopy equivalent to a point. Euclidean space ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is the primordial example of an open contractible manifold: radially contract every point to the origin.

The history of open contractible manifolds is closely intertwined with the history of geometric topology. To explain this connection, recall that the classical Poincaré conjecture asks whether every closed manifold MnM^{n} homotopy equivalent to SnS^{n} is actually homeomorphic to SnS^{n}. The history of the Poincaré conjecture is closely connected with the history of open contractible manifolds.

In 1934, J.H.C. Whitehead gave what he thought was a proof of the Poincaré conjecture in dimension 33 [Whi34]. In brief, his argument went as follows: start with a homotopy equivalence f:M3⟶S3f:M^{3}\longrightarrow S^{3}. Removing a point produces an open contractible manifold M3∖p​tM^{3}\smallsetminus pt and continuous map f:M3∖p​t→ℝ3f:M^{3}\smallsetminus pt\to{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. In essence, Whitehead argued that all open contractible 33-manifolds are homeomorphic to ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. If this was true, then such a homeomorphism would extend by continuity across infinity inducing a homemorphism M3→S3M^{3}\rightarrow S^{3}. Unfortunately, this proof collapsed soon thereafter as Whitehead constructed an open contractible manifold 𝒲\mathcal{W} (the so-called Whitehead manifold) that is not homeomorphic to the Euclidean space ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} [Whi35]. Whitehead’s example raised the question of characterizing Euclidean space among all open contractible manifolds, perhaps in some homotopic way.

Whitehead’s construction is delightfully geometric and is given as an open subset of a Euclidean space with closed complement the “Whitehead continuuum”, itself built out of intricately linked tori. Since the construction of the Whitehead manifold is relatively simple, we give it here. Consider the Whitehead link in S3S^{3}; thicken it to obtain two linked solid tori; label the interior solid torus T^1\hat{T}_{1} and the exterior solid torus T0T_{0}. The complement of each TiT_{i} in S3S^{3} is unknotted. Since T^1\hat{T}_{1} is unknotted, the complement T1T_{1} of the interior of T^1\hat{T}_{1} in S3S^{3} is another unknotted solid torus that contains T0T_{0}. Choose a homeomorphism hh of S3S^{3} that maps T0T_{0} onto T1T_{1}. Proceeding inductively, may therefore construct solid tori T0⊂T1⊂⋯T_{0}\subset T_{1}\subset\cdots in S3S^{3} by setting Tj+1=h⁡(Tj)T_{j+1}=h(T_{j}). The union 𝒲:=∪iTi\mathcal{W}:=\cup_{i}T_{i} is the required open contractible manifold. To see that 𝒲\mathcal{W} is simply connected, one proceeds as follows. Observe that every closed loop in M3M^{3} is contained in some TjT^{j} by construction. Now, observe that every closed loop in T0T_{0} may be shrunk to a point (possibly crossing through itself) in T1T^{1}, and thus every closed loop in TjT_{j} may be shrunk to a point in Tj+1T_{j+1}.

Whitehead’s original proof that 𝒲\mathcal{W} is not homeomorphic to ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is essentially geometric. However, it was later observed that for any sufficiently large compact subset K⊂𝒲K\subset\mathcal{W} (KK contains T0T_{0} suffices), the complement 𝒲∖K{\mathcal{W}}\smallsetminus K is not simply connected. More generally, suppose MM is an open contractible manifold. We may consider the collection of compact sets K⊂MK\subset M ordered with respect to inclusion. In good situations, the inverse system π1​(M∖K)\pi_{1}(M\smallsetminus K) stabilizes and defines an invariant of the homeomorphism type of MM called the fundamental group at infinity and denoted π1∞​(M)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(M). Observe that ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is simply-connected at infinity, since any compact subset is contained in a sufficiently large ball, whose complement in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} is simply connected.

While Whitehead’s construction lay dormant for some time, open contractible manifolds were studied with great intensity in the late 1950s and 1960s. Although 𝒲\mathcal{W} is not homeomorphic to ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3} Glimm and Shapiro pointed out that the cartesian product 𝒲×ℝ1\mathcal{W}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{1} is homeomorphic to ℝ4{\mathbb{R}}^{4} [Gli60], i.e., 𝒲\mathcal{W} does not have the cancellation property with respect to Cartesian products with Euclidean spaces. Moreover, Glimm showed that the self-product 𝒲×𝒲\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{W} is homeomorphic to ℝ6{\mathbb{R}}^{6} [Gli60]. These kinds “non-cancellation” phenomenon become another theme explored in the study of open contractible manifolds.

By modifying the construction of the Whitehead continuum, D.R. McMillan constructed infinitely many pairwise non-homeomorphic open contractible 33-manifolds [McM62]; each of these 33-manifolds could be embedded in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. While McMillan’s original proof that his manifolds were non-homeomorphic was essentially geometric, it was observed that his examples actually have distinct fundamental groups at infinity. This naturally raises the question of which groups may appear as a fundamental groups at infinity of open contractible 33-manifolds.

Simultaneously, McMillan showed his examples also had the property that taking a Cartesian product with the real line yielded a manifold homeomorphic to ℝ4{\mathbb{R}}^{4}. In fact, McMillan showed that the product of any open contractible 33-manifold MM and the real line was homeomorphic to ℝ4{\mathbb{R}}^{4} assuming the 33-dimensional Poincaré conjecture. Later joint work of J. Kister and McMillan [KM62] established existence of open contractible 33-manifolds that could not be embedded in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. Work of Zeeman and McMillan then showed that the product of any open contractible 33-manifold and ℝ2{\mathbb{R}}^{2} was homeomorphic to ℝ5{\mathbb{R}}^{5}. From one point of view, the zoo of open contractible manifolds presented some kind of “lower bound” on the complexity of the Poincaré conjecture.

The existence of open contractible manifolds of higher dimensions was also studied in conjunction with the higher dimensional Poincaré conjecture. Constructions of open contractible 44-manifolds were initially given by Mazur and Poenaru [Maz61, Poe60], but as with many other constructions in geometric topology, these isolated examples in dimension 44 did not at first fit into a general picture. Dimension ≥5\geq 5 proved itself to be more tractable. Extending the results of McMillan, for any integer n≥5n\geq 5, Curtis and Kwun [CK65] constructed uncountably many pairwise non-homeomorphic open contractible nn-manifolds.

The method of Curtis and Kwun in some sense mirrors McMillan’s construction, but requires significantly more group theoretic input. The basic idea is to construct open contractible manifolds with a prescribed (finitely presented) fundamental group at infinity. If PP is a finitely presented group, then one may build many cell complexes K⁡(P)K(P) with fundamental group PP. If one embeds K⁡(P)K(P) in SnS^{n} for n≥5n\geq 5, then the boundary of a regular neighborhood NN of K⁡(P)K(P) has fundamental group PP (this fails for n=4n=4, since the fundamental group of the boundary depends on the embedding). One says that K⁡(P)K(P) is a homologically trivial presentation if Hi​(K​(P),ℤ)H_{i}(K(P),{\mathbb{Z}}) is trivial for i=1,2i=1,2. In particular, if PP admits a homologically trivial presentation then the Hurewicz theorem implies that K⁡(P)K(P) is a perfect group. If NN is a regular neighborhood of an embedding K⁡(P)↪SnK(P)\hookrightarrow S^{n}, n≥5n\geq 5, then one sees that Sn∖∂NS^{n}\smallsetminus\partial N is contractible if K⁡(P)K(P) is a homologically trivial presentation, but has fundamental group at infinity PP. The output is that one has countably many compact contractible manifolds that act as “building blocks” for an uncountable collection by taking suitable connected sums. The method of Curtis and Kwun for producing “building blocks” evidently does not extend to n=4n=4. Later, Glaser extended Mazur’s construction to produce countably many “building blocks” from which uncountably many pairwise non-homeomorphic open contractible 44-manifolds could be built by taking suitable connected sums as above [Gla67]. We summarize these results in the following statement.

Theorem 1.

In every dimension ≥3\geq 3, there exists uncountably many pairwise non homeomorphic open contractible nn-manifolds.

Returning to non-cancellation phenomena, Stallings [Sta62] generalized the results of Zeeman and McMillan by observing:

  1. 1.

    for any integer n≥5n\geq 5, ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is the unique open contractible P​LPL-manifold that is simply-connected at infinity; and

  2. 2.

    if MnM^{n} is an open contractible mm-manifold, then Mn×ℝM^{n}\times{\mathbb{R}} is always simply-connected at infinity.

These observations tamed the zoo of open contractible manifolds in some sense. The homotopical characterization of Euclidean space above is sometimes called the open Poincaré conjecture. Stallings’ result was later generalized by Siebenmann [Sie68] to yield an essentially homotopical characterization of the Euclidean space amongst all open contractible topological nn-manifolds. In conjunction with more recent work on the low-dimensional Poincaré conjecture, i.e., the celebrated work of Perelman [Car14] and Freedman [Mil97], Siebenmann’s theorem can be extended to the following statement.

Theorem 2.

Suppose n≥0n\geq 0 is an integer.

  1. 1.

    For n≤2n\leq 2, Euclidean space ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is the unique open contractible nn-manifold.

  2. 2.

    For n≥3n\geq 3, Euclidean space ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is the unique open contractible nn-manifold that is simply connected at infinity.

  3. 3.

    If n≥3n\geq 3, and MM is an open contractible nn-manifold, then M×ℝM\times{\mathbb{R}} is homeomorphic to ℝn+1{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}.

The modern study of open manifolds formalizes the notion of “behavior at ∞\infty” of an open manifold as follows. If WW is a topological space, we write W˙\dot{W} for a 11-point compactification of WW. Write [0,∞][0,\infty] for the extended real line (i.e., with a limit point at infinity). The end space e⁡(W)e(W) consists of the space of maps of pairs ω:([0,∞],{∞})→(W˙,{∞})\omega:([0,\infty],\{\infty\})\to(\dot{W},\{\infty\}) such that ω−1​(∞)=∞\omega^{-1}(\infty)=\infty [HR96, §1, Definition 1.2]. The end space may be viewed as a homotopy theoretic model for the behaviour at ∞\infty of WW. If WW is already compact, then W˙=W+\dot{W}=W_{+}, so the end space is empty. The end space may not be connected: e⁡(ℝ)e({\mathbb{R}}) is homotopy equivalent to S0S^{0} corresponding to the two infinite simple edge paths starting at 0∈ℝ0\in{\mathbb{R}}. More generally, e⁡(ℝn)≃Sn−1e({\mathbb{R}}^{n})\simeq S^{n-1}. In that case, we will say that WW is simply connected at infinity if e⁡(W)e(W) is connected and simply connected.

1.2 Contractible algebraic varieties

Cancellation questions like those mentioned above were also studied in algebraic geometry, though in several different contexts. Perhaps the first such question was posed by Zariski [Seg50]: if kk is a field, LL and L′L^{\prime} are finitely generated extensions of kk such that the purely transcendental extensions L⁡(x)L(x) and L′​(x)L^{\prime}(x) are isomorphic as extensions of kk, are LL and L′L^{\prime} isomorphic? Phrased in the language of algebraic geometry: if XX and X′X^{\prime} are irreducible algebraic varieties over a field kk such that X×ℙ1X\times{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}} is kk-birationally equivalent to X′×ℙ1X^{\prime}\times{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}, is XX kk-birational to X′X^{\prime}? At some point, in the late 1960s/early 1970s, a closely related “biregular” form of Zariski’s original cancellation question was posed: if AA and BB are finitely generated kk-algebras, and A⁡[x]≅B⁡[x]A[x]\cong B[x] as kk-algebras, is A≅BA\cong B? Even at the beginning, special attention was paid to the case where AA is a polynomial ring. M.P. Murthy [Ram71] also asked: if AA is a Krull dimension 22 extension of a field kk and A⁡[x]≅k⁡[x1,x2,x3]A[x]\cong k[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}], then must AA be a polynomial ring in 22-variables? In the language of algebraic geometry this leads to the following question.

Question 3 (Biregular cancellation question).

If XX is a smooth affine variety over a field such that X×𝔸n≅𝔸NX\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{N}, then is XX isomorphic to affine space?

Remark 4.

The more general cancellation question will be of interest to us as well, and we refer the reader to Sections 3.3 and 3.4 for more discussion and history of these kinds of questions. The above question is also sometimes called the “Zariski cancellation problem”, but it appears never to have been explicitly posed or considered by Zariski.

The situation surrounding Question 3 is quite different depending on the characteristic. Over fields of positive characteristic, recent work of N. Gupta, building on some old ideas of Asanuma [Asa99] exploiting interesting pathologies existing only in positive characteristic produced counterexamples to the biregular cancellation question [Gup14a]. Nevertheless, at the time of writing, the question is still open over fields having characteristic 00.

From the outset, ideas of topology played a role in approaches to the biregular cancellation problem over fields having characteristic 00. If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, then we write Xa​nX^{an} for the set X⁡(ℂ)X({\mathbb{C}}) equipped with its usual structure of a complex manifold. More generally, if kk is a field for which we can find an embedding ι:k↪ℂ\iota:k\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}, then we may use ι\iota to define an associated complex manifold Xιa​nX^{an}_{\iota}. If kk is a field that admits a complex embedding, then we will say that XX is topologically contractible if Xιa​nX^{an}_{\iota} is a contractible space for every complex embedding ι\iota of kk. The variety 𝔸kn{\mathbb{A}}^{n}_{k} is the primordial example of a topologically contractible variety. Thus, any complex variety that is stably isomorphic to 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} is also automatically topologically contractible. Bearing this in mind, we would like to place the discussion of the biregular cancellation question in context using the theory of open contractible manifolds as a template.

Ramanujam writes in [Ram71] that it was initially hoped that a 22-dimensional non-singular, affine, rational, topologically contractible complex variety would be isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. However, he constructs a counter-example to this hope in his landmark paper–a surface now called the Ramanujam surface in his honor; we briefly recall the construction of the Ramanujam surface. Ramanujam also gave a topological characterization of the affine plane among complex algebraic varieties: ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} is the unique non-singular contractible complex surface that is simply connected at infinity.

Example 5.

In ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} take a cubic CC with a cusp at qq. Let QQ be an irreducible conic meeting CC with multiplicity 55 at a point pp and transversally at a point rr. The existence of QQ can be deduced from the group law on the non-singular part of CC, or directly by avoiding that pp is a flex-point of CC. Let XX be the blow-up of ℙ2{\mathbb{P}}^{2} at rr and let C~\tilde{C}, Q~\tilde{Q} denote the strict transforms of CC, QQ, respectively. The Ramanujam surface is defined by setting

ℛ=X∖C~∪Q~.\mathcal{R}=X\smallsetminus\tilde{C}\cup\tilde{Q}.

Smooth complex varieties XX that are not isomorphic to 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} but for which Xa​nX^{an} is diffeomorphic to ℝ2​n{\mathbb{R}}^{2n} are known as exotic affine spaces. Such varieties are automatically topologically contractible; for a survey we refer the reader to [Zaĭ99]. After the work of Ramanujam, many examples of topologically contractible smooth varieties were invented; for example, see the work of tom Dieck and Petrie [tDP90] for examples given by explicit equations. In fact, there is a veritable zoo of such examples: there exist arbitrary dimensional moduli of topologically contractible smooth complex affine surfaces!

The biregular cancellation problem was later solved in the affirmative for surfaces by Miyanishi–Sugie [MS80] and Fujita [Fuj79] in characteristic 00 and Russell in positive characteristic: the affine plane (over an algebraically closed field) is the unique surface that is stably isomorphic to an affine space (see Section 5.1 for precise references).

Ramanujam’s topological characterization of the affine plane also fails to hold in higher dimensions. Indeed, Dimca and Ramanujam both proved that if XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine variety of dimension d≥3d\geq 3, then XX is automatically diffeomorphic to ℝ2​d{\mathbb{R}}^{2d}. Putting these facts together, one sees that there are many exotic affine varieties in dimensions ≥3\geq 3: simply take the products of topologically contractible surfaces and affine spaces! This observation, together with the fact that “topological” invariants do not always have natural counterparts in positive characteristic, suggest that one might hope for a purely algebraic theory of contractible varieties that is more refined than the topological notion discussed here. Nevertheless, there are a great number of questions about the geometry of topologically contractible varieties that one may pose here, and we highlight several questions that have guided the development of the theory of contractible algebraic varieties.

Question 6 (Generalized Serre Question).

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine variety, then is every algebraic vector bundle on XX trivial?

Remark 7.

This question is called the generalized Serre question in the literature [Zaĭ99, §8] and we have followed this terminology here. To the best of our knowledge, Serre only ever considered this question for affine space over a field [Ser55, p. 243], where it spectacularly resolved (independently) by Quillen and Suslin [Qui76, Sus76]; we refer the reader to [Lam06] for a nice survey of these results. Of course, it is based on the fact that complex topological vector bundles on contractible varieties are trivial. We will see later that the affineness assumption in the question is essential; see Example 3.5.4 for more details.

Question 8 (Generalized van de Ven question).

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex variety, then is XX rational?

Remark 9.

This question is sometimes referred to as the van de Ven Question in the literature [Zaĭ99, Remark 2.2] with reference given to [vdV62]. We call it the generalized van de Ven question because van de Ven was explicitly concerned with surfaces: he writes [vdV62, §3 p.197-198] “All the known examples of algebraic non-singular compactifications of homology 22-cells are rational surfaces. It would follow that there are no others, at least if we restrict ourselves to simply connected homology 22-cells, if the following statement would be true: (ℭ)({\mathfrak{C}}) Every simply connected non-singular algebraic surface with geometric genus 00 is rational.” Unfortunately, the conjecture (ℭ)({\mathfrak{C}}) was later disproved: for example the Barlow surfaces [Bar85] are simply connected surfaces of general type with geometric genus 00. Nevertheless, Gurjar and Shastri showed [GS89a, GS89b] that non-singular contractible surfaces are always rational by a careful case-by-case analysis.

A theorem of Fujita shows that all topologically contractible smooth complex surfaces are necessarily affine. A remarkable example of Winkelmann [Win90] shows that Fujita’s statement does not hold in higher dimensions. Winkelmann gave the first example of a quasi-affine but not affine smooth contractible complex variety.

Example 10.

Winkelmann defines a scheme-theoretically free action of the additive group 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} on 𝔸5{\mathbb{A}}^{5} as follows. Consider the standard 22-dimensional representation VV of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} given by the embedding 𝔾a↪S​L2\mathbb{G}_{a}\hookrightarrow SL_{2} as upper triangular matrices. The 66-dimensional affine space attached to V⊕V⊕VV\oplus V\oplus V thus carries a linear representation of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}. If we pick coordinates x0,x1x_{0},x_{1}, y0,y1y_{0},y_{1} and z0,z1z_{0},z_{1} on this affine space, then x0x_{0}, y0y_{0} and z0z_{0} are degree 11 invariant functions, while x0​y1−y0​x1x_{0}y_{1}-y_{0}x_{1}, x0​z1−z0​x1x_{0}z_{1}-z_{0}x_{1} and y0​z1−z0​y1y_{0}z_{1}-z_{0}y_{1} are degree 22 invariants. The hypersurface x0=1−y0​z1−z0​y1x_{0}=1-y_{0}z_{1}-z_{0}y_{1} is thus a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-invariant smooth hypersurface in 𝔸6{\mathbb{A}}^{6} isomorphic to 𝔸5{\mathbb{A}}^{5}. The induced action is scheme-theoretically free, and invariant computation just mentioned identifies the quotient as an open subscheme of a smooth affine quadric of dimension 44 with complement a codimension 22 affine space.

Winkelmann’s example highlights another important issue in algebraic geometry that is not visible in the topological story. Indeed, it follows from the theorems we stated before that every open contractible manifold may be realized as a quotient of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} by a free action of the additive group ℝ{\mathbb{R}}. However, every principal ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-bundle on a topological space having the homotopy type of a CW-complex is trivial because ℝ{\mathbb{R}} is contractible. In contrast, in algebraic geometry, a natural analog of free ℝ{\mathbb{R}}-actions on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is given by (scheme-theoretically) free actions of the additive group scheme 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} on 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}. One must first ask then: given a scheme-theoretically free action of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}, when does a quotient even exist as a scheme (a quotient always exists as an algebraic space)? If XX is a scheme, then the set of isomorphism classes of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-torsors on XX is parameterized by the sheaf cohomology group H1​(X,𝔾a)=H1​(X,𝒪X)H^{1}(X,\mathbb{G}_{a})=H^{1}(X,\mathscr{O}_{X}). On an affine scheme, this cohomology group necessarily vanishes, but it need not vanish on a quasi-affine scheme that is not affine.

Example 10 gives the primordial example of a smooth variety that is “algebraically” homotopy equivalent to affine space, without being isomorphic to affine space. While there are various “naive” notions of algebraic homotopy equivalence (e.g., one may think of homotopies parameterized by the affine line), a robust homotopy theory for algebraic varieties in which homotopies are parameterized by the affine line requires more formal machinery. In the sequel, we begin by trying to highlight the key points of one solution–the construction of the Morel–Voevodsky 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy [MV99]–from the standpoint of the tools required by an end user interested in algebro-geometric questions like those posed above. Section 2 contains motivation and the basic ideas of the construction, without going into any of the formal categorical preliminaries. In Section 3, we try to understand concretely and geometrically how to study isomorphisms in the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category, a.k.a. 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. In the context of the discussion above, we introduce the key notion of an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible space, see Definition 3.1.1. In what remains, we review the theory of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth varieties, guided by the discussion above, especially the theory of open-contractible manifolds. Along the way, we discuss an algebro-geometric version of Theorem 1.

Theorem 11 (See Theorems 3.5.2 and 5.4.3).

Assume kk is a field. For every pair of integers d≥3d\geq 3 and n≥0n\geq 0, there exists a connected nn-dimensional scheme SS and a smooth morphism π:X→S\pi:X\to S of relative dimension dd whose fibers are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. Moreover, the fibers over distinct kk-points of π\pi are pairwise non-isomorphic.

Much of the rest of the discussion can be viewed as providing background for the following questions, which suggest a best-possible approximation to an algebro-geometric variant of Theorem 2 (see Definition 3.3.1 for the terminology).

Question 12.

If kk is a perfect field, is 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} the only 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth kk-scheme of dimension ≤2\leq 2?

Question 13.

Suppose XX is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme.

  1. 1.

    Does there exist an affine space 𝔸N{\mathbb{A}}^{N} and a Nisnevich locally trivial smooth morphism 𝔸N→X{\mathbb{A}}^{N}\to X?

  2. 2.

    If XX is moreover affine, then is XX a retract of 𝔸N{\mathbb{A}}^{N}?

The first question above is discussed in detail in Section 5.2. The second is motivated by the discussion of Section 3.5 in conjunction with the discussion of Sections 3.3, 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5. Finally, we suggest that there is a rather subtle relationship between topologically contractible varieties and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties involving “suspension” in the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category.

Conjecture 14 (See Conjecture 5.3.11).

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex variety with a chosen base-point x∈X⁡(ℂ)x\in X({\mathbb{C}}), then there exists an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that Σℙ1n​(X,x)\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible; in fact, n=2n=2 should suffice.

As with any survey, this one reflects the knowledge and biases of the authors. The literature in affine algebraic geometry on cancellation and related questions is vast, and we can only apologize to those authors whose work we have (inadvertently) failed to appropriately credit.

2 A user’s guide to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory

We began by stating a slogan, loosely paraphrasing the first section of [MV99]:

there should be a homotopy theory for algebraic varieties over a base where the affine line plays the role assigned to the unit interval in topology.

The path to motivate the construction of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category that we follow is loosely based on the work of Dugger [Dug01]. The original constructions of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category rely on [Jar87] and are to be found in [MV99]. General overviews of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory may be found in [Voe98], and, especially for “unstable” results in [Mor06]. Morel’s paper [Mor04] provides an introductory text, but recent advances like [AHW17] and [HKØ15] allow one to get to the heart of the matter much more quickly. We encourage the reader to consult [AE17], [IØ18], [Lev16], and [WW19] for recent surveys.

2.1 Brief topological motivation

The jumping off point for the discussion was the classical Brown-representability theorem in unstable homotopy theory. Recall that the ordinary homotopy category, denoted here ℋ{\mathscr{H}}, has as objects “sufficiently nice” topological spaces Top\mathrm{Top} (including, for example, all CW complexes), and morphisms given by homotopy classes of continuous maps between spaces. Unfortunately, the category of CW complexes itself is not “categorically good” enough to build the homotopy category. Indeed, there are various constructions one wants to perform in topology (quotients, loop spaces, mapping spaces, suspensions) that do not stay in the category of CW complexes (they only stay in the category up to homotopy). We will refer to objects of the category Top\mathrm{Top} (which we have not precisely specified) as spaces. As usual, for two spaces XX and YY, we write [X,Y][X,Y] for the set of morphisms between XX and YY in the homotopy category.

Suppose 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a category of “algebraic structures”. In practice, one may take 𝐂\mathbf{C} to be the category of sets or an abelian category like abelian groups, or chain complexes, but we will need some flexibility in the choice. A 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued invariant is then a contravariant functor ℱ:Top→𝐂{\mathcal{F}}:\mathrm{Top}\to\mathbf{C}. We will furthermore consider 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued invariants on Top\mathrm{Top} that satisfy the following properties:

  • i)

    (Homotopy invariance axiom) If XX is a topological space, and I=[0,1]I=[0,1] is the unit interval, then the map ℱ⁡(X)→ℱ⁡(X×I){\mathcal{F}}(X)\to{\mathcal{F}}(X\times I) is a bijection.

  • ii)

    (Mayer-Vietoris axiom) If XX is a CW complex covered by subcomplexes UU and VV with intersection U∩VU\cap V, then we have a diagram of the form

    ℱ⁡(X)→ℱ⁡(U)×ℱ⁡(V)→ℱ⁡(U∩V),{\mathcal{F}}(X)\to{\mathcal{F}}(U)\times{\mathcal{F}}(V)\to{\mathcal{F}}(U\cap V),

    and given u∈ℱ⁡(U)u\in{\mathcal{F}}(U) and v∈ℱ⁡(V)v\in{\mathcal{F}}(V), such that the images of uu and vv under the right hand map coincide, then there is an element of ℱ⁡(X){\mathcal{F}}(X) whose image under the first map is the pair (u,v)(u,v).

  • iii)

    (Wedge axiom) The functor ℱ{\mathcal{F}} takes sums to products.

Given a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued invariant ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on Top\mathrm{Top} as above, the first condition implies that ℱ{\mathcal{F}} factors through a functor ℋ→𝐂\mathscr{H}\to\mathbf{C}, i.e., ℱ{\mathcal{F}} is a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued homotopy invariant. There is a very natural class of representable Set\operatorname{Set}-valued homotopy invariants, given by [−,Y][-,Y] for some topological space YY. Given a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued homotopy invariant ℱ{\mathcal{F}}, the classical Brown representability theorem says that if it satisfies the second and third conditions above, then this functor is a representable homotopy invariant, i.e., there is a CW complex YY and an isomorphism of functors ℱ≅[−,Y]\mathscr{F}\cong[-,Y].

Remark 2.1.1.

In general, “cohomology theories” satisfy more properties than just those mentioned: e.g., one has a Mayer–Vietoris long exact sequence. For example, consider the functor sending a space to its usual integral singular cochain complex S∗​(X)S^{*}(X). If XX is a topological space, then S∗​(X)→S∗​(X×I)S^{*}(X)\to S^{*}(X\times I) is not an isomorphism of chain complexes, but a chain-homotopy equivalence. Likewise, if X=U∪VX=U\cup V, then there is a sequence

S∗​(X)⟶S∗​(U)⊕S∗​(V)⟶S∗​(U∩V),S^{*}(X)\longrightarrow S^{*}(U)\oplus S^{*}(V)\longrightarrow S^{*}(U\cap V),

but this sequence fails to be an exact sequence of chain complexes. To get a Mayer–Vietoris sequence one must replace S∗​(X)S^{*}(X) by a suitable subcomplex with the same cohomology. These observations necessitate making various constructions that are “homotopy invariant” from the very start.

Remark 2.1.2.

If a “cohomology theory” is represented on CW complexes by a space ZZ, and the cohomology theory is geometrically defined (e.g., topological K-theory with ZZ the infinite grassmannian), then the “representable” cohomology theory extended to all topological spaces need not coincide with the geometric definition for spaces that are not CW complexes.

2.2 Homotopy functors in algebraic geometry

We would like to guess what properties the “homotopy category” will have based on the known invariance properties of cohomology theories in algebraic geometry. To this end, we must have some actual “cohomology theories” at hand. The examples we want to use are the theory of Chow groups [Ful98] and (higher) algebraic K-theory [Qui73], though the reader not familiar with general definitions could focus on the Picard group, which is related to both. We begin by formulating a notion of homotopy invariance in algebraic geometry. As above, suppose 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a category of algebraic structures.

Definition 2.2.1.

A 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued contravariant functor ℱ{\mathcal{F}} on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant if the morphism ℱ⁡(U)→ℱ⁡(U×𝔸1){\mathcal{F}}(U)\to{\mathcal{F}}(U\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}) is a bijection.

Example 2.2.2.

The functor P​i​c​(X)Pic(X) is not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant on schemes with singularities that are sufficiently complicated [Tra70]. More generally, Chow groups are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant [Ful98, Theorem 3.3] for regular schemes. Likewise, Grothendieck established an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariance property for algebraic K0K_{0} on regular schemes, and Quillen established a homotopy invariance property for algebraic K-theory of regular schemes (this is one of the fundamental properties of higher algebraic K-theory proven in [Qui73]).

In the examples above, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariance, failed to hold on all schemes. As a consequence, we restrict our attention to the category Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} of schemes that are separated, smooth and have finite type over kk (we use smooth schemes rather than regular schemes since smoothness is more functorially well-behaved than regularity; if we assume we work with varieties over a perfect field, then there is no need to distinguish between the two notions). Our restriction to smooth schemes will be analogous to the restriction to (finite) CW complexes performed above.

We would like to impose some Mayer–Vietoris-like condition on 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued invariants. The most obvious choice would involve the Zariski topology on schemes. In practice, a number of classical algebro-geometric cohomology theories have a Mayer–Vietoris property for a Grothendieck topology that is finer than the Zariski topology. Indeed, Chow groups and algebraic K-theory have “localization” exact sequences; we review such sequences here as a motivation for the finer topology.

Let us recall the localization sequence for Chow groups: if XX is a smooth variety, and U⊂XU\subset X is an open subvariety with closed complement ZZ (say equi-dimensional of codimension dd), there is an exact sequence of the form

C​H∗−d​(Z)⟶C​H∗​(X)⟶C​H∗​(U)⟶0;CH^{*-d}(Z)\longrightarrow CH^{*}(X)\longrightarrow CH^{*}(U)\longrightarrow 0;

to extend this sequence further to the left, one needs to introduce Bloch higher Chow groups [Blo86, Blo94], but we avoid discussing this here. We leave the reader the exercise of showing that from this localization sequence, one may formally deduce that Chow groups and algebraic K-theory have a suitable Mayer–Vietoris property for Zariski open covers by two sets.

One often considers the étale topology in algebraic geometry, and one might ask whether there is an appropriate Mayer-Vietoris sequence for étale covers. In this direction, consider the following situation. Suppose given an open immersion j:U↪Xj:U\hookrightarrow X and an étale morphism φ:V→X\varphi:V\to X such that the pair (j,φ)(j,\varphi) are jointly surjective and such that the induced map φ−1​(X∖U)→X∖U\varphi^{-1}(X\smallsetminus U)\to X\smallsetminus U is an isomorphism, diagrammatically this is a picture of the form:

We will refer to such diagrams as Nisnevich distinguished squares. One can show that XX is the colimit in the category of smooth schemes of the diagram U⟵U×XV⟶VU\longleftarrow U\times_{X}V\longrightarrow V.

By a straight-forward diagram chase, one may show that the sequence

C​H∗​(X)→C​H∗​(U)⊕C​H∗​(V)→C​H∗​(U×XV)CH^{*}(X)\to CH^{*}(U)\oplus CH^{*}(V)\to CH^{*}(U\times_{X}V)

is exact: given an element (u,v)(u,v) in C​H∗​(U)⊕C​H∗​(V)CH^{*}(U)\oplus CH^{*}(V), if the restriction of (u,v)(u,v) to C​H∗​(U×XV)CH^{*}(U\times_{X}V) is zero, then there is an element xx in C​H∗​(X)CH^{*}(X) whose restriction to C​H∗​(U)⊕C​H∗​(V)CH^{*}(U)\oplus CH^{*}(V) is (u,v)(u,v). Therefore, any theory that satisfies localization will have the Mayer–Vietoris property with respect to a Grothendieck topology on schemes that is finer than the Zariski topology.

Example 2.2.3.

Suppose kk is a field of characteristic unequal to 22. Consider the diagram where X=𝔸1X={\mathbb{A}}^{1}, U=𝔸1∖{1}U={\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{1\}, V=𝔸1∖{0,−1}V={\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,-1\}. Let jj be the usual open immersion of 𝔸1∖{1}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{1\} into 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, and let φ\varphi be the étale map given by the composite 𝔸1∖{0,−1}↪𝔾m→𝔾m↪𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,-1\}\hookrightarrow{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, where the map 𝔾m→𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} is z↦z2z\mapsto z^{2}. It is easily checked that this diagram provides a square as above.

To define a homotopy category for smooth schemes, informed by the above observations, we will attempt to build a category through which any 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy invariant on smooth schemes satisfying Mayer–Vietoris in the Nisnevich sense prescribed above factors. We do this in a few stages. Just as the category of CW-complexes was not “categorically good”, we will first enlarge the category of schemes to a suitable category of spaces. Then, we will force Mayer–Vietoris for Nisnevich covers and then impose 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy invariance.

Remark 2.2.4.

As is hopefully evident, we have made a number of choices here: a category of schemes with which to begin, and a topology for which we would like to impose Mayer–Vietoris; we have motivated a particular choice here, but other choices are often warranted. For example, we might want to make constructions involving non-smooth schemes and be able to compare this situation with the one we alluded to above. For this reason, we will try to leave some flexibility in the constructions.

2.3 The unstable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category: construction

Spaces

For concreteness, fix a base Noetherian commutative unital ring kk of finite Krull dimension. In practice, kk will be a field, but for comparing constructions in different characteristics, it will often be useful for kk to be a discrete valuation ring or the integers ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}. Write Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} for the category of schemes that are separated, smooth and have finite type over kk. Write Schk\mathrm{Sch}_{k} for the category of Noetherian kk-schemes of finite Krull dimension. Write sSet\mathrm{sSet} for the category of simplicial sets. There is a functor Set→sSet\operatorname{Set}\to\mathrm{sSet} sending a set SS to the corresponding constant simplicial set (i.e., all face and degeneracy maps are the identity), and we use this functor to identify Set\operatorname{Set} as a full subcategory of sSet\mathrm{sSet}.

Definition 2.3.1.

Write Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} for the category of simplicial presheaves on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k}, and Spck′\mathrm{Spc}_{k}^{\prime} for the category of simplicial presheaves on Schk\mathrm{Sch}_{k}; objects of these categories will be called motivic spaces or kk-spaces, depending on whether we want to explicitly specify kk.

Sending a (smooth) scheme to its corresponding representable presheaf (of constant simplicial sets) defines a functor Schk→Spck′\mathrm{Sch}_{k}\to\mathrm{Spc}_{k}^{\prime} (Smk→Spck\mathrm{Sm}_{k}\to\mathrm{Spc}_{k}) that is fully-faithful by the Yoneda lemma. We use these functors without mention to identity (smooth) schemes as spaces. Likewise, there is a functor sSet→Spck\mathrm{sSet}\to\mathrm{Spc}_{k} sendin a simplicial set to the corresponding constant simplicial presheaf.

There are many constructions we may perform in the category of spaces: these categories are both complete and cocomplete, i.e., have limits and colimits indexed by all small categories. The category Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} (resp. Spck′\mathrm{Spc}_{k}^{\prime}) has a final object typically denote ∗\ast and an inital object ∅\emptyset. Using the fact that Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} has all small limits and colimits, the following definitions make sense. A pointed space is a pair (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) where 𝒳∈Spck\mathscr{X}\in\mathrm{Spc}_{k} and x:∗→𝒳x:\ast\to\mathscr{X} is a morphism of spaces. We write Spck,∙\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet} for the category of pointed kk-spaces. It is important to emphasize that these constructions are being made in the category of spaces and NOT in the category of schemes. Moreover, moving outside of the category of schemes has a number of tangible benefits.

  • •

    If (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) and (𝒴,y)({\mathscr{Y}},y) are pointed kk-spaces, then the wedge sum 𝒳∨𝒴\mathscr{X}\vee\mathscr{Y} is the pushout (colimit) of the diagram 𝒳⟵x∗⟶y𝒴\mathscr{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle x}}{{\longleftarrow}}\ast\stackrel{{\scriptstyle y}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathscr{Y}.

  • •

    If (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) and (𝒴,y)({\mathscr{Y}},y) are pointed kk-spaces, then the smash product 𝒳∧𝒴\mathscr{X}\wedge\mathscr{Y} is the quotient of 𝒳×𝒴/𝒳∨𝒴\mathscr{X}\times\mathscr{Y}/{\mathscr{X}}\vee\mathscr{Y}.

  • •

    We write SiS^{i} for the constant presheaf with value ∂Δi+1\partial\Delta^{i+1}, where Δi+1\Delta^{i+1} is the usual i+1i+1-simplex.

Nisnevich and cdh distinguished squares

We now make precise various ideas given above motivated by Mayer–Vietoris sequences.

Definition 2.3.2.

A Nisnevich distinguished square is a pull-back diagram of schemes

such that j:U↪Xj:U\hookrightarrow X is an open immersion, φ:V→X\varphi:V\to X is an étale morphism, and the induced map φ−1​(X∖U)→X∖U\varphi^{-1}(X\smallsetminus U)\to X\smallsetminus U is an isomorphism of schemes given the reduced induced scheme structure.

Remark 2.3.3.

Every Zariski open cover of a scheme by two open sets gives rise to a Nisnevich distinguished square. Nisnevich distinguished squares generate a Grothendieck topology on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} or Schk\mathrm{Sch}_{k} called the Nisnevich topology. This topology is conveniently described in terms of covering sieves: it is the coarsest topology such that the empty sieve covers ∅\emptyset, and for every distinguished square as above, the sieve on XX generated by U→XU\to X and V→XV\to X is a covering sieve. This definition of the Nisnevich topology is equivalent to other standard ones in the literature. In fact, the Nisnevich topology may be generated by much simpler squares where all corners of the square are affine and the reduced closed complement of UU in XX is given by a principal ideal. We refer the interested reader to [AHW17, §2] for more details.

For the most part, we will only use Nisnevich distinguished squares and the Nisnevich topology, but the following definition will also be useful.

Definition 2.3.4.

An abstract blow-up square is a pull-back diagram of schemes of the form:

where ii is a closed immersion, π\pi is a proper map, and the induced map π−1​(X∖i⁡(Z))→X∖i⁡(Z)\pi^{-1}(X\smallsetminus i(Z))\to X\smallsetminus i(Z) is an isomorphism.

Remark 2.3.5.

As above, the proper cdh topology on Schk\mathrm{Sch}_{k} is the coarsest topology such that the empty sieve covers ∅\emptyset, and for which the sieve on XX generated by Z→XZ\to X and Y→XY\to X is a covering sieve. The cdh topology is the smallest Grothendieck topology whose covering morphisms include those of the proper cdh topology and those of the Nisnevich topology.

Localization

Given the category Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} (resp. Spck′\mathrm{Spc}^{\prime}_{k}), we now want to formally invert a set of morphisms 𝒮\mathscr{S} to build a homotopy category. Each covering sieve of a Grothendieck topology gives rise to a monomorphism of presheaves with target a representable presheaf; to impose “Mayer–Vietoris” with respect to a given topology, one first formally inverts the set of all of these monomorphisms. Concretely, if u:U→Xu:U\to X is a Nisnevich covering, then one may build a simplicial presheaf C˘​(U)\breve{C}(U) by taking iterated fiber products of UU with itself over XX. The morphism uu then yields an augmentation

C˘​(U)⟶X\breve{C}(U)\longrightarrow X

that we would like to force to be a weak equivalence. The Nisnevich (resp. cdh) local homotopy category is, in essence, the universal category where the above maps have been inverted (see [AHW17, Lemma 3.1.3] for a precise statement). There are numerous constructions of this category now and the “universal” point-of-view espoused here was studied in great detail by D. Dugger; see [Dug01] for more details.

One standard way to invert the relevant set of morphisms is to equip Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} (resp. Spck′\mathrm{Spc}_{k}^{\prime}) with the structure of model category (see, e.g., [Hov99]); this involves specifying classes of cofibrations and fibrations along with the classes of morphisms that are to be inverted, i.e., the morphisms we want to become weak equivalences. In any case, we will write HNis​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\operatorname{Nis}}}(k) (resp. Hc​d​h​(k)\mathrm{H}_{cdh}(k)) for the corresponding local homotopy category; we refer the reader to [Jar15] for a textbook treatment of local homotopy theory. By construction, there is a functor Spck→HNis​(k)\mathrm{Spc}_{k}\to\mathrm{H}_{{\operatorname{Nis}}}(k) (resp. Spck′→Hc​d​h​(k)\mathrm{Spc}_{k}^{\prime}\to\mathrm{H}_{cdh}(k) that is suitably (i.e., homotopically) initial.

One may build 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy categories in a similar universal fashion. After formally inverting Nisnevich (resp. cdh) local weak equivalences, we further invert the projection from the affine line:

𝒳×𝔸1⟶𝒳.\mathscr{X}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\longrightarrow\mathscr{X}.

We write H𝔸1​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(k) for the corresponding category obtained by localizing HNis​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\operatorname{Nis}}}(k) and H𝔸1c​d​h​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}^{cdh}(k) for the category obtained by localizing Hc​d​h​(k)\mathrm{H}_{cdh}(k).

Notation 2.3.6.

An isomorphism in H𝔸1​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(k) or H𝔸1c​d​h​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}^{cdh}(k) will be called an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. To emphasize the analogy with topology, we write [𝒳,𝒴]𝔸1[\mathscr{X},{\mathscr{Y}}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} for the set of morphisms in either category; we will read this as the set of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy classes of maps between 𝒳\mathscr{X} and 𝒴\mathscr{Y}.

Remark 2.3.7.

Given 𝒳\mathscr{X} and 𝒴\mathscr{Y} in Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k} and a morphism H:𝒳×𝔸1→𝒴H:\mathscr{X}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to\mathscr{Y}, we may think of HH as an algebraic homotopy between H⁡(−,0):𝒳→𝒴H(-,0):\mathscr{X}\to\mathscr{Y} and H⁡(−,1):𝒳→𝒴H(-,1):\mathscr{X}\to\mathscr{Y}; we will say that H⁡(−,0)H(-,0) and H⁡(−,1)H(-,1) are naively homotopic. More generally, we will say that two morphisms 𝒳→𝒴\mathscr{X}\to\mathscr{Y} are naively homotopic if they are equivalent for the equivalence relation generated by naive homotopies. Note that naively homotopic maps determine the same 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy class, i.e., there is an evident function

HomSpck⁡(𝒳,𝒴)/{naive ​𝔸1​-homotopies}⟶[𝒳,𝒴]𝔸1,\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Spc}_{k}}(\mathscr{X},\mathscr{Y})/\{\text{naive }{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\text{-homotopies}\}\longrightarrow[\mathscr{X},\mathscr{Y}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}},

but this morphism is rarely a bijection.

2.4 The unstable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category: basic properties

Motivic spheres

In addition to the simplicial circle S1S^{1} described above, we introduce the Tate circle 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}, viewed as a space pointed by the identity section. We then define bigraded motivic spheres by the formula

Si,j=Si∧𝔾m∧j.S^{i,j}=S^{i}\wedge{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}j}}.

From these definitions, and basic homotopy-invariance statements, one may write down some standard algebro-geometric models of motivic spheres. Homotopy categories typically do not have robust notions of limit or colimit, and one therefore considers a more flexible “up to homotopy” notion. The results below are straightforward homotopy colimit computations, and we mention the required facts without going into details.

Example 2.4.1.

The space 𝔸1/{0,1}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}/\{0,1\} is a model for S1S^{1}. This is an algebro-geometric analog of the fact that the circle S1S^{1} can be realized as the homotopy pushout of the two-point space S0S^{0} along the maps projecting onto each point.

One of the basic consequences of our construction of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category is that any Zariski Mayer–Vietoris square is a pushout square.

Example 2.4.2.

There is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence S1,1≅ℙ1S^{1,1}\cong{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. To see this, use the standard Zariski open cover of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} by two copies of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}.

Example 2.4.3.

There is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence 𝔸n∖0≅Sn−1,n{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0\cong S^{n-1,n}. Use induction and the open cover of 𝔸n∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0 by the open sets (𝔸n−1∖0)×𝔸1({\mathbb{A}}^{n-1}\smallsetminus 0)\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} and 𝔾m×𝔸n−1{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n-1} with intersection 𝔾m×(𝔸n−1∖0){{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\times({\mathbb{A}}^{n-1}\smallsetminus 0).

Example 2.4.4.

There is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence ℙn/ℙn−1≅Sn,n{\mathbb{P}}^{n}/{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\cong S^{n,n}. Use the open cover of ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n} by 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} and ℙn∖0{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0 with intersection 𝔸n∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0.

Remark 2.4.5.

With reference to Definition 4.1.3 we remark that Si,jS^{i,j} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-(i−1)(i-1)-connected in the sense that the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy sheaf 𝝅n𝔸1​(Si,j)\bm{\pi}_{n}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(S^{i,j}) vanishes for n≤i−1n\leq i-1, see [Mor06, §3]. This corresponds precisely to the connectivity of the real points of Si,jS^{i,j}.

Representability statements

Just like in topology, there is a Brown representability theorem characterizing homotopy functors in algebraic geometry. In addition to homotopy invariance, one wants functors that turn Nisnevich distinguished squares into “homotopy” fiber products; for more details, see the works of Jardine [Jar11] and Naumann-Spitzweck [NS11]. One additional subtlety that arises is that many natural functors of algebro-geometric origin that arise fail to be 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant on the category of all smooth schemes. Thus, one would also like to investigate representability questions for such functors. We summarize some theorems that will be useful in the sequel.

In topology, complex line bundles are represented by homotopy classes of maps to infinite complex projective space, at least on spaces having the homotopy type of a CW complex. There is an algebro-geometric analog of this result. For any base commutative unital ring kk, one may define the space ℙk∞{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}_{k} as the colimit of ℙkn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}_{k} along the standard closed immersions ℙn↪ℙn+1{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{n+1}. The space ℙ∞{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty} can be given a multiplication in the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category. Indeed, the Segre embeddings ℙn×ℙm⟶ℙ(n+1)​(m+1)−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{m}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{(n+1)(m+1)-1} may be used to define a map ℙ∞×ℙ∞→ℙ∞{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}. This multiplication map may be shown to be associative up to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy and equips [−,ℙ∞]𝔸1[-,{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}} with a group structure. In the algebro-geometric setting, one has a representability theorem for algebraic line bundles.

Proposition 2.4.6 ([MV99, §4 Proposition 3.8]).

If kk is a regular ring, then for any smooth kk-scheme XX, there is an isomorphism of the form

P​i​c​(X)⟶∼[X,ℙ∞]𝔸1;Pic(X){\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\;\longrightarrow\;}}}[X,{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}};

this isomorphism is functorial in XX.

In topology, complex vector bundles of a given rank are represented by homotopy classes of maps to a suitable infinite Grassmannian, at least on spaces having the homotopy type of a CW complex. Unfortunately, the functor assigning to a smooth scheme XX over a base kk the set 𝒱r​(X)\mathscr{V}_{r}(X) of isomorphism classes of rank rr vector bundles on XX fails to be 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant, as the following example shows. Thus, this functor cannot be representable on the category of all smooth schemes.

Example 2.4.7.

Consider ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. A classical result of Dedekind–Weber often attributed to Grothendieck asserts that all vector bundles on ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} are direct sums of line bundles (see [HM82] for an elementary proof). Consider X=ℙ1×𝔸1X={\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} with coordinates tt and xx. The matrix

(t−1x0t)\begin{pmatrix}t^{-1}&x\\ 0&t\end{pmatrix}

is the clutching function for a rank 22 vector bundle on ℙ1×𝔸1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. The fiber over x=0x=0 of this bundle is isomorphic to 𝒪⁡(−1)⊕𝒪⁡(1)\mathscr{O}(-1)\oplus\mathscr{O}(1), while the fiber over x=1x=1 (or any other non-zero value) is isomorphic to 𝒪⊕𝒪\mathscr{O}\oplus\mathscr{O}. This rank 22 vector bundle is therefore evidently not pulled back from a vector bundle on ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}.

A classical result of Lindel [Lin82] shows that the functor 𝒱r​(X)\mathscr{V}_{r}(X) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant upon restriction to the category of smooth affine kk-schemes, if kk is a field. This result was extended by Popescu to the case where kk is a Dedekind domain with perfect residue fields. Then, even though 𝒱r​(X)\mathscr{V}_{r}(X) fails to be representable on all smooth schemes, one can hope it is representable on smooth affine schemes. On smooth affine schemes, given a vector bundle, one may always choose generating sections, i.e., every vector bundle is determined by a morphism to a Grassmannian. We may define G​rnGr_{n} as a space to be the colimit of G​rn,NGr_{n,N} over standard inclusions G​rn,N→G​rn,N+1Gr_{n,N}\to Gr_{n,N+1}.

Theorem 2.4.8 (Morel, Schlichting, Asok–Hoyois–Wendt).

If kk is smooth over a Dedekind ring with perfect residue fields, then for any smooth affine kk-scheme XX, there is a pointed bijection

[X,G​rr]𝔸1≅𝒱r​(X);[X,Gr_{r}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\cong\mathscr{V}_{r}(X);

this bijection is functorial in XX.

Comments on the proof.

This result was stated originally by F. Morel [Mor12, Theorem 8.1] in the case where kk is perfect and assuming r≠2r\neq 2. Morel’s argument was greatly simplified by M. Schlichting [Sch17, Theorem 6.22]. The result appears in the form above in [AHW17, Theorem 1]. ∎

Remark 2.4.9.

While vector bundles of a given rank are only representable on smooth affine schemes, upon passing to stable isomorphism classes, i.e., algebraic K-theory, one may obtain a representability statement on all smooth schemes. Representability of algebraic K-theory was first established in [MV99, Theorem 3.13], though we refer the reader to [ST15, Remark 2 p. 1162] for some corrections to the original argument.

Representability of Chow groups

Chow cohomology groups are also representable on smooth schemes, but the representing object is a bit more subtle. To set the stage recall that ordinary singular cohomology with coefficients in an abelian group AA is representable on finite CW-complexes by Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces K⁡(A,n)K(A,n). A classical result of Dold and Thom gives a concrete geometric model for the Eilenberg–Mac Lane space K⁡(ℤ,n)K({\mathbb{Z}},n). Indeed for a pointed topological space TT, we may define the symmetric product S​y​mn​(T)Sym^{n}(T) as the quotient of the nn-fold product by the action of the symmetric group on nn letters permuting the factors, i.e.,

S​y​mn​(T)=Tn/Σn.Sym^{n}(T)=T^{n}/\Sigma_{n}.

Using the base-point, there are natural inclusions S​y​mn​T→S​y​mn+1​TSym^{n}T\to Sym^{n+1}T, and one defines the infinite symmetric product S​y​m​(T)Sym(T) as the colimit of the finite symmetric powers with respect to these inclusions. The space S​y​m​(T)Sym(T) may be thought of as the free commutative monoid on TT. By “group completing,” we may define a space S​y​m​(T)+Sym(T)^{+} that is a topological abelian group. For connected spaces, the group completion process does not alter the homotopy type, and the classical Dold–Thom theorem shows that for every n≥0n\geq 0, there are weak equivalences of the form:

K⁡(ℤ,n)≅S​y​m​(Sn),K({\mathbb{Z}},n)\cong Sym(S^{n}),

i.e., Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces may be realized as infinite symmetric products of spheres.

The procedure sketched above yields a reasonable representing model for Chow groups as well. For a smooth scheme XX, define a presheaf ℤt​r​(X){\mathbb{Z}}_{tr}(X) on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} by assigning to U∈SmkU\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k} the free abelian group on irreducible closed subschemes of U×XU\times X that are finite and surjective over a component of UU. This construction is covariantly functorial in XX as well, and for a closed subscheme Z⊂XZ\subset X, we define ℤt​r​(X/Z)=ℤt​r​(X)/Zt​r​(Z){\mathbb{Z}}_{tr}(X/Z)={\mathbb{Z}}_{tr}(X)/Z_{tr}(Z), where the latter quotient is the quotient as presheaves of abelian groups. In particular, we saw earlier that ℙn/ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n}/{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} is a model of the motivic sphere Sn,nS^{n,n}, and we set

K⁡(ℤ⁡(n),2​n):=ℤt​r​(ℙn/ℙn−1).K({\mathbb{Z}}(n),2n):={\mathbb{Z}}_{tr}({\mathbb{P}}^{n}/{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}).

The spaces K⁡(ℤ⁡(n),2​n)K({\mathbb{Z}}(n),2n) are usually called motivic Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces. With that definition in mind, we can formulate the appropriate representability theorem.

Theorem 2.4.10 ([Del09]).

Assume kk is a perfect field. For every n≥0n\geq 0, and every smooth kk-scheme XX, there are canonical bijections

[X+,K⁡(ℤ⁡(n),2​n)]𝔸1⟶C​Hn​(X).[X_{+},K({\mathbb{Z}}(n),2n)]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\longrightarrow CH^{n}(X).
Remark 2.4.11.

We refer the reader to [Voe03b, §2] for a convenient summary of properties of motivic cohomology phrased in terms of motivic Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces. The relationship between K⁡(ℤ⁡(n),2​n)K({\mathbb{Z}}(n),2n) and symmetric products, which may appear a bit obscure above stems from the link between symmetric powers and algebraic cycles on quasi-projective varieties; we refer the interested reader to [Voe98, §6.1] and the references therein for more details. This relationship is perhaps most clearly seen in the case n=1n=1 where C​H1​(X)=P​i​c​(X)CH^{1}(X)=Pic(X). One may define S​y​mnSym^{n} on the category of (say) quasi-projective varieties over a field. It is well-known that ℙn≅S​y​mn​(ℙ1){\mathbb{P}}^{n}\cong Sym^{n}({\mathbb{P}}^{1}) as schemes (essentially, this is the map sending a polynomial in 11 variable to its roots). Thus, S​y​m​(ℙ1)≅ℙ∞Sym({\mathbb{P}}^{1})\cong{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}. Using this identification, one may build a map ℙ∞→K⁡(ℤ⁡(1),2){\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}\to K({\mathbb{Z}}(1),2); this map is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

The purity isomorphism

Definition 2.4.12.

If XX is a smooth scheme and π:E→X\pi:E\to X is a vector bundle with zero section i:X→Ei:X\to E, we define T​h​(π)=E/E−i⁡(X)Th(\pi)=E/E-i(X).

This definition of Thom space has many of the same properties as the corresponding construction in topology; we summarize some here.

Proposition 2.4.13.

Suppose XX is a smooth scheme.

  1. 1.

    If π:X×𝔸n→X\pi:X\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\to X is a trivial bundle of rank nn, then T​h​(π)≅ℙ1∧n∧X+Th(\pi)\cong{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}\wedge X_{+}.

  2. 2.

    If ψ:X′→X\psi:X^{\prime}\to X is a morphism of schemes, π′:E′→X′\pi^{\prime}:E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} is a vector bundle on X′X^{\prime} and π:E→X\pi:E\to X is a vector bundle on XX fitting into a commutative square of the form

    then there is an induced morphism T​h​(π′)→T​h​(π)Th(\pi^{\prime})\to Th(\pi).

  3. 3.

    If π:E→X\pi:E\to X and π′:E′→X\pi^{\prime}:E^{\prime}\to X are vector bundles over XX, then T​h​(π⊕π′)≅T​h​(π)∧T​h​(π′)Th(\pi\oplus\pi^{\prime})\cong Th(\pi)\wedge Th(\pi^{\prime}).

The importance of the notion of Thom space stems from the purity isomorphism, which we summarize in the next result. For later use, we will need to understand functoriality of purity isomorphism. In order to precisely formulate the functoriality properties, we need to introduce a bit of terminology. Suppose we have a cartesian square of smooth schemes of the form

where ii is a closed immersion. In that case, i′i^{\prime} is also a closed immersion and we will say the square is transversal if the induced map of normal bundles φ:νZ′/X′→f∗​νZ/X\varphi:\nu_{Z^{\prime}/X^{\prime}}\to f^{*}\nu_{Z/X} is an isomorphism. The following result was established in [MV99, §3 Theorem 2.23]; the subsequent functoriality statements appear in [Voe03a, §2].

Theorem 2.4.14 (Homotopy purity).

Suppose kk is a Noetherian ring of finite Krull dimension.

  1. 1.

    If i:Z→Xi:Z\to X is a closed immersion of smooth kk-schemes, then there is a purity isomorphism

    X/X−i⁡(Z)≅T​h​(νi).X/X-i(Z)\cong Th(\nu_{i}).
  2. 2.

    If i:Z→Xi:Z\to X is the zero section of a geometric vector bundle π:X→Z\pi:X\to Z, then the purity isomorphism is the identity map.

  3. 3.

    Given a transversal diagram of smooth schemes as above, the purity isomorphism is functorial in the sense that there is a commutative square of the form

    where the horizontal maps are the purity isomorphisms, the left vertical map is the map on quotients induced by commutativity of the square and the right vertical map is the map induced by functoriality of Thom spaces.

Remark 2.4.15.

As will become clear in the sequel, homotopy purity is an absolutely fundamental tool in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, especially from the standpoint of computations. In the context of stable categories to be introduced in Section 2.5 it will lead to Gysin exact sequences.

Comparison of Nisnevich and cdh-local 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences

There is an obvious inclusion Smk→Schk\mathrm{Sm}_{k}\to\mathrm{Sch}_{k}; this yields a functor Spck′→Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k}^{\prime}\to\mathrm{Spc}_{k} by restriction. One may show that there is an induced (derived) “pullback” functor π∗:H𝔸1​(k)→H𝔸1c​d​h​(k)\pi^{*}:\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(k)\to\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}^{cdh}(k). For later use, we will need the following comparison theorem of Voevodsky [Bla01, Theorem 5.1] [Voe10, Theorem 4.2].

Theorem 2.4.16 (Voevodsky).

Assume kk is a field having characteristic 00. Suppose f:(𝒳,x)→(𝒴,y)f:(\mathscr{X},x)\to(\mathscr{Y},y) is a pointed morphism in Spck\mathrm{Spc}_{k}. If π∗​(f)\pi^{*}(f) is an isomorphism in H𝔸1c​d​h​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}^{cdh}(k), then Σ​f\Sigma f is an isomorphism in H𝔸1​(k)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(k).

2.5 A snapshot of the stable motivic homotopy category

One of the basic lessons of classical homotopy theory is that calculations become more accessible after inverting the suspension functor on the homotopy category of pointed spaces. The notion of a topological spectrum makes this process precise [Ada74]. Similar constructions turn out to be extremely useful in the setting of motivic homotopy theory following [DRØ03], [Hov01], [Jar00], [Mor04], [Voe98].

For the purposes of this survey it is useful to know there exists a closed symmetric monoidal category 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) called the stable motivic homotopy category of the field kk. We note that 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) is an additive category, in fact a triangulated category equipped with the auto-equivalence given by smashing with the simplicial circle. This category is obtained by formally inverting suspension with the projective line ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} on the category Spck,∙\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet} of pointed motivic spaces. One formally inverts ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} by considering “spectra”. A motivic spectrum E∈SptkE\in\mathrm{Spt}_{k} is comprised of pointed motivic spaces EnE_{n} for all n≥0n\geq 0 together with structure maps ℙ1∧En→En+1\mathbb{P}^{1}\wedge E_{n}\to E_{n+1}. For example, every X∈SmkX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k} has an associated motivic suspension spectrum Σℙ1∞​X+\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+} with terms (ℙ1)∧n∧X+(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{\wedge n}\wedge X_{+} and identity structure maps. Reminiscent of the way the natural numbers give rise of the integers we are entitled to motivic spheres Sp,qS^{p,q} in 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) for all p,q∈ℤp,q\in{\mathbb{Z}}. In fact, 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) is generated by shifted motivic suspension spectra of the form Σp,q​Σℙ1∞​X+\Sigma^{p,q}\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+}. With a great deal of tenacity one can make precise the statement that 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) is the associated stable homotopy category of Sptk\mathrm{Spt}_{k}. Moreover, one can define a symmetric monoidal structure on 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) for which the sphere spectrum 𝟏=Σℙ1∞​Spec⁡(k)+{\mathbf{1}}=\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\operatorname{Spec}(k)_{+} is the unit.

There are standard Quillen adjunctions, whose left adjoints preserve weak equivalences

Σℙ1:Spck,∙⇄Spck,∙:Ωℙ1\displaystyle\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}:\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet}\rightleftarrows\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet}:\Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}
Σℙ1∞:Spck,∙⇄Sptk:Ωℙ1∞.\displaystyle\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}:\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet}\rightleftarrows\mathrm{Spt}_{k}:\Omega^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}.

Moreover, we let ℋ​o​m​(E,F){\mathcal{H}om}(E,F) denote the internal homomorphism object of 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k) characterized by the adjunction isomorphism

Hom𝒮​ℋ​(k)⁡(D,ℋ​o​m​(E,F))≃Hom𝒮​ℋ​(k)⁡(D∧E,F).\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(k)}(D,{\mathcal{H}om}(E,F))\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(k)}(D\wedge E,F).

Later on in our discussion of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility we will appeal to the following result connecting the stable and unstable worlds of motivic homotopy theory. We include a proof since it illustrates some basic concepts and techniques.

Lemma 2.5.1.

Let XX be a smooth scheme and x∈Xx\in X a closed point. If Σℙ1∞(X,x)≃∗\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x)\simeq\ast in 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k), then there exists an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that Σℙ1n​(X,x)\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

Proof.

By [DRØ03, Definition 2.10], an object F∈Spck,∙F\in\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet} is fibrant exactly when for every X∈SmkX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k}, (1) F⁡(X)F(X) is a Kan complex; (2) the projection X×𝔸1→XX\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to X induces a homotopy equivalence F⁡(X)≃F⁡(X×𝔸1)F(X)\simeq F(X\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}); (3) FF maps Nisnevich elementary distinguished squares in Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} to homotopy pullback squares of simplicial sets, and F⁡(∅)F(\emptyset) is contractible. Moreover, a motivic spectrum E∈SptkE\in\mathrm{Spt}_{k} is fibrant if and only if it is levelwise fibrant and an Ωℙ1\Omega_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}-spectrum.

Let (En)n≥0(E_{n})_{n\geq 0} be a levelwise fibrant replacement of Σℙ1∞​(X,x)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x), i.e., EnE_{n} is a fibrant replacement of Σℙ1n​(X,x)\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) in Spck,∙\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet}, and let EE be a fibrant replacement of Σℙ1∞​(X,x)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) in Sptk\mathrm{Spt}_{k}. A key observation is that filtered colimits in Spck,∙\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet} preserve fibrant objects; this follows from the above description of fibrant objects and the facts that filtered colimits of simplicial sets preserve Kan complexes, homotopy equivalences, and homotopy pullback squares ([DRØ03, Corollary 2.16]). Putting these facts together, one deduces that there is a simplicial homotopy equivalence

Ωℙ1∞​E≃colimn→∞⁡Ωℙ1n​En.\Omega^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}E\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{n\to\infty}\Omega^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}E_{n}.

Let X~∈Spck,∙\tilde{X}\in\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet} be the simplicial presheaf (X,x)∨Δ1(X,x)\vee\Delta^{1} pointed at the free endpoint of Δ1\Delta^{1}; this is a cofibrant replacement of (X,x)(X,x) in Spc∙​(k)\mathrm{Spc}_{\bullet}(k). Since X~∈Spck,∙\tilde{X}\in\mathrm{Spc}_{k,\bullet} is ω\omega-compact, the following are homotopy equivalences of Kan complexes, where Map\operatorname{Map} denotes the simplicial sets of maps in the above simplicial model categories

Map⁡(Σℙ1∞​X~,E)\displaystyle\operatorname{Map}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X},E) ≃Map⁡(X~,Ωℙ1∞​E)\displaystyle\simeq\operatorname{Map}(\tilde{X},\Omega^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}E)
≃Map⁡(X~,colimn→∞⁡Ωℙ1n​En)\displaystyle\simeq\operatorname{Map}(\tilde{X},\operatorname{colim}_{n\to\infty}\Omega^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}E_{n})
≃colimn→∞⁡Map⁡(X~,Ωℙ1n​En)\displaystyle\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Map}(\tilde{X},\Omega^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}E_{n})
≃colimn→∞⁡Map⁡(Σℙ1n​X~,En).\displaystyle\simeq\operatorname{colim}_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{Map}(\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X},E_{n}).

The hypothesis that Σℙ1∞​(X,x)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) is weakly contractible means that the weak equivalence Σℙ1∞​X~→∼E\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}E and the zero map Σ∞ℙ1X~→∗→E\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X}\to*\to E are in the same connected component of the Kan complex Map⁡(Σℙ1∞​X~,E)\operatorname{Map}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X},E). Since π0\pi_{0} preserves filtered colimits of simplicial sets, there exists an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that the weak equivalence Σℙ1n​X~→∼En\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\to}}E_{n} and the zero map Σnℙ1X~→∗→En\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X}\to*\to E_{n} belong to the same connected component of Map⁡(Σℙ1n​X~,En)\operatorname{Map}(\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X},E_{n}). In other words, Σℙ1n​X~≃Σℙ1n​(X,x)\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\tilde{X}\simeq\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. ∎

Milnor–Witt K-theory

For later reference we recall the definition of Milnor-Witt KK-theory 𝐊∗M​W​(k){{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{*}(k) in [Mor12]. It is the quotient of the free associative integrally graded ring on the set of symbols [k×]:={[u]∣u∈k×}[k^{\times}]:=\{[u]\mid u\in k^{\times}\} in degree 11 and η\eta in degree −1-1 by the homogeneous ideal imposing the relations

  • (1)

    [u​v]=[u]+[v]+η⁡[u]​[v][uv]=[u]+[v]+\eta[u][v] (η\eta-twisted logarithm),

  • (2)

    [u]​[v]=0[u][v]=0 for u+v=1u+v=1 (Steinberg relation),

  • (3)

    [u]​η=η⁡[u][u]\eta=\eta[u] (commutativity), and

  • (4)

    (2+[−1]​η)​η=0(2+[-1]\eta)\eta=0 (hyperbolic relation).

Milnor-Witt KK-theory is ε\varepsilon-commutative for ε=−(1+[−1]​η)\varepsilon=-(1+[-1]\eta). By work of Morel there is an isomorphism with the graded ring of endomorphisms of the sphere

𝐊∗M​W​(k)≅⨁n∈ℤπn,n​𝟏.{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{*}(k)\cong\bigoplus_{n\in{\mathbb{Z}}}\pi_{n,n}{\mathbf{1}}.

Moreover, we have 𝐊0M​W​(k)≅G​W​(k){{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{0}(k)\cong GW(k), the Grothendieck-Witt ring of stable isomorphism classes of symmetric bilinear forms [MH73]. Inverting η\eta in 𝐊∗M​W​(k){{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{*}(k) yields the ring of Laurent polynomials W​(k)​[η±1]W(k)[\eta^{\pm 1}] over the Witt ring, and 𝐊∗M​W​(k)/η≅𝐊∗M​(k){{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{*}(k)/\eta\cong{{\mathbf{K}}}^{M}_{*}(k), the Milnor KK-theory ring of kk [Mil70].

Stable representablity of algebraic K-theory

Algebraic KK-theory is also representable in the stable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category. To see this, it suffices to consider the infinite projective space ℙ∞{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty} and a certain “Bott element” β\beta obtained from the virtual vector bundle [𝒪]−[𝒪⁡(−1)][\mathscr{O}]-[\mathscr{O}(-1)] over ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}. The precise context involves the stable motivic homotopy category 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k); we replace ℙ∞{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty} with its motivic suspension spectrum Σℙ1∞​ℙ+∞\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}_{+} upon which it makes sense to invert β\beta.

Theorem 2.5.2 (Gepner–Snaith, Spitzweck–Østvær).

If kk is a noetherian ring with finite Krull dimension, then there is a natural isomorphism in 𝒮​ℋ​(k)\mathscr{SH}(k)

Σℙ1∞​ℙ+∞​[β−1]≅𝐊𝐆𝐋.\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}{\mathbb{P}}^{\infty}_{+}[\beta^{-1}]\cong{\mathbf{KGL}}.
Comments on the proof.

Here 𝐊𝐆𝐋{\mathbf{KGL}} is the algebraic KK-theory spectrum introduced by Voevodsky [Voe98]. Independent proofs of this result are given in [GS09] and [SØ09]. The conclusion holds more generally over any noetherian base scheme of finite Krull dimension. ∎

3 Concrete 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences

In this section, we attempt to make the discussion of the previous section more concrete. In particular, we will discuss fundamental examples of isomorphisms in the unstable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category. Moreover, we recall some results from affine (and quasi-affine) algebraic geometry in the context of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory.

3.1 Constructing 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences of smooth schemes

By construction of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category, for any smooth scheme XX the projection map X×𝔸1→XX\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to X is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence; in particular, the morphism 𝔸1→Spec⁡k{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to\operatorname{Spec}k is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. By induction, one concludes that 𝔸n→Spec⁡k{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\to\operatorname{Spec}k is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. In fact, one may give a completely algebraic construction of this 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence using the ideas of Remark 2.3.7. Indeed, there is a morphism 𝔸1×𝔸n→𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n} sending (t,x1,…,xn)↦(t​x1,…,t​xn)(t,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\mapsto(tx_{1},\ldots,tx_{n}); this corresponds to the usual radial rescaling map. As in topology, this construction defines a naive 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy between the identity map (t=1t=1) and the map factoring through the inclusion of 00 (t=1t=1). In any case, affine space gives the first example of a space satisfying the hypotheses of the following definition.

Definition 3.1.1.

A space 𝒳∈Spck\mathscr{X}\in\mathrm{Spc}_{k} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible if the structure morphism 𝒳→Spec⁡k\mathscr{X}\to\operatorname{Spec}k is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Example 3.1.2.

Assume kk is a field and let α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} be coprime integers. The cuspidal curve Γα1,α2={yα1−zα2=0}\Gamma_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}=\{y^{\alpha_{1}}-z^{\alpha_{2}}=0\} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible. More precisely, we identify Γα1,α2\Gamma_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}} as a motivic space by restricting its functor of points to Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k}. Then, the normalization map 𝔸x1→Γα1,α2\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}\to\Gamma_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}} given by x↦(xα2,xα1)x\mapsto(x^{\alpha_{2}},x^{\alpha_{1}}) is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-weak equivalence, even an isomorphism of presheaves on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} (see [AD07, Example 2.1]).

Suppose ZZ is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme. Since we have forced maps that are “Nisnevich locally” weak equivalences to be weak equivalences, it follows that any map that is Nisnevich locally isomorphic to the product projection U×Spec⁡kZ→UU\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}Z\to U is automatically a weak equivalence. More precisely, if f:X→Yf:X\to Y is a morphism of smooth kk-schemes, and there exists a Nisnevich covering map u:U→Yu:U\to Y and an isomorphism of UU-schemes X×YU≅U×Spec⁡kZX\times_{Y}U\cong U\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}Z, then we will say that ff is Nisnevich locally trivial with 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible fibers.

Lemma 3.1.3.

If f:X→Yf:X\to Y is any morphism of smooth kk-schemes that is Nisnevich locally trivial with affine space fibers, then ff is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Any morphism ff of smooth schemes that is Nisnevich locally trivial with affine space fibers is automatically an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. For example, the projection map in a geometric vector bundle is automatically a vector bundle. More generally, if π:E→X\pi:E\to X is a torsor under a vector bundle on XX, then π\pi is Zariski locally trivial (this folows from the vanishing of coherent cohomology on affine schemes), and thus an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. Jouanolou originally observed [Jou73] that given a quasi-projective variety XX, one could find a torsor under a vector bundle over XX whose total space was affine; such a scheme will be called an affine vector bundle torsor. Thomason generalized this observation to schemes admitting an ample family of line bundles; and in the next result we summarize the consequences for 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory.

Lemma 3.1.4 (Jouanolou–Thomason homotopy lemma).

If kk is a regular ring, and XX is a separated, finite type, smooth kk-scheme, then there exists a smooth affine kk-scheme X~\tilde{X} and morphism π:X~→X\pi:\tilde{X}\to X that is a torsor under a vector bundle; in particular, π:\pi: is Zariski locally trivial with affine space fibers and is thus an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

Proof.

If kk is regular, then XX is a separated, regular, Noetherian scheme. In that case, XX admits an ample family of line bundles (combine [SGA71, Expose III Corollaire 2.2.7.1]. The result then follows from [Wei89, Proposition 4.4], a result attributed to Thomason. ∎

Remark 3.1.5.

If XX is a smooth scheme, then a choice of smooth affine scheme X~\tilde{X} and an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence π:X~→X\pi:\tilde{X}\to X will be called a Jouanolou device over XX. Unfortunately, the construction of Jouanolou devices is not functorial.

Example 3.1.6.

For any base ring kk, following Jouanolou, there is a very simple example of a Jouanolou device over ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}. Let ℙn~\widetilde{{\mathbb{P}}^{n}} be the complement of the incidence hyperplane in ℙn×ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{n} (viewing the second ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n} as the dual of the first). It is easy to see that the composite of the inclusion and the projection onto the first factor defines a morphism ℙn~→ℙn\widetilde{{\mathbb{P}}^{n}}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{n} which is a Jouanolou device; we will refer to this as the standard Jouanolou device over ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}. For n=1n=1 it is straighforward to check that ℙ1~\widetilde{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}} is isomorphic to the closed subscheme of 𝔸k3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}_{k} defined by the equation x​y=z⁡(1+z)xy=z(1+z).

3.2 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences vs. weak equivalences

For this section, we will consider rings kk that come equipped with a homomorphism ι:k→ℂ\iota:k\to{\mathbb{C}}. In that case, we may compare 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences and classical weak equivalences via what are often called “realization functors”. Given a smooth kk-scheme XX, we may consider the set Xιa​nX^{an}_{\iota} (via ι\iota) and we view this as a complex manifold with its usual structure. Morel and Voveodsky [MV99, §3.3] show that the assignment X↦Xιa​nX\mapsto X^{an}_{\iota} may then be extended to a functor between homotopy categories
