ℜι:ℋ⁡(k)⟶ℋ{\mathfrak{R}}_{\iota}:\mathscr{H}({k})\longrightarrow\mathcal{H}

which we refer to as a (topological) realization functor; see [DI04] for more discussion of topological realization functors. In particular, applying ℜι{\mathfrak{R}}_{\iota} to an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence of smooth schemes yields a weak equivalence of the associated topological spaces of complex points.

Remark 3.2.1.

The choice ι\iota is important: Serre showed that it is possible to find smooth algebraic varieties over a number field together with two embeddings of kk into ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that the resulting complex manifolds are homotopy inequivalent. In fact, F. Charles provided examples of two smooth algebraic varieties over a number field kk together with two embeddings of kk into ℂ{\mathbb{C}} such that the real cohomology algebras of the resulting complex manifolds are not isomorphic [Cha09]. Said differently, the real homotopy type of a smooth kk-scheme may depend on the choice of embedding of kk into ℂ{\mathbb{C}}.

Question 3.2.2.

Assume ι1,ι2:k→ℂ\iota_{1},\iota_{2}:k\to{\mathbb{C}} are distinct ring homomorphisms. Is it possible to find a (smooth) kk-scheme XX such that ℜι1​(X)\mathfrak{R}_{\iota_{1}}(X) is contractible while ℜι2​(X)\mathfrak{R}_{\iota_{2}}(X) is not?

Remark 3.2.3.

Recall that a connected topological space XX is ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic if Hi​(X,ℤ)=0H_{i}(X,{\mathbb{Z}})=0 for all i>0i>0. Of course, contractible topological spaces are ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic. One can show that the property of being ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-acyclic is independent of the choice of embedding for smooth varieties using étale cohomology as follows. If XX is a smooth kk-scheme, then the integral singular cohomology groups Hi​(Xa​n,ℤ)H_{i}(X^{an},{\mathbb{Z}}) are finitely generated abelian groups. By the Artin-Grothendieck comparison theorem, the cohomology of X⁡(ℂ)X({\mathbb{C}}) with ℤ/n{\mathbb{Z}}/n-coefficients is isomorphic to the étale cohomology of XX with ℤ/n{\mathbb{Z}}/n-coefficients, and étale cohomology of XX is independent of the choice of embedding of kk into ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. By appeal to the universal coefficient theorem, one deduces that the vanishing of Hi​(Xa​n,ℤ)t​o​r​sH_{i}(X^{an},{\mathbb{Z}})_{tors} for one embedding implies the vanishing for any other. Similarly, the rank of the free part is determined by the Betti numbers, which are also determined by étale cohomology and are therefore also independent of the choice of embedding.

To our knowledge, all the examples where homotopy types change with the embedding involve a nontrivial fundamental group. If XX is a topologically contractible smooth kk-scheme, then its étale fundamental group is independent of the choice of embedding. Furthermore, the étale fundamental group of XX is the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group of X⁡(ℂ)X({\mathbb{C}}). Thus, if XX is topologically contractible, then any of the manifolds X⁡(ℂ)X({\mathbb{C}}) has a fundamental group with trivial profinite completion. If one could prove that X⁡(ℂ)X({\mathbb{C}}) has trivial fundamental group for any choice of embedding, the above problem would have a positive solution as a consequence of the usual Whitehead theorem. Let us also note that, working with étale homotopy types, one can deduce restrictions on the profinite completions of the other homotopy groups of X⁡(ℂ)X({\mathbb{C}}).

Using the realization functor mentioned above and the definition of topologically contractible varieties from the introduction, the following result is immediate.

Lemma 3.2.4.

If kk is a commutative ring, ι:k→ℂ\iota:k\to{\mathbb{C}} is a homomorphism, and XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth kk-scheme, then ℜι​(X)\mathfrak{R}_{\iota}(X) is topologically contractible.

Remark 3.2.5.

While complex realization is only available for fields admitting an embedding in ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, there are other realization functors that may be defined more generally. For example, one may define an étale realization functor on the unstable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category over any field [Isa04]. Over fields having characteristic pp, the pp-part of the étale homotopy type is not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant in general. For example, the affine line over a separably closed field having positive characteristic has a large nontrivial étale fundamental group. Thus, étale realization of an unstable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type involves completion away from the residue characteristics of whatever base ring we work over. Correspondingly, the analog of Lemma 3.2.4 says that the étale realization of an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme is only trivial after a suitable completion. On the other hand, the true “topological” analog of contractibility, i.e., contractibility in the étale sense including triviality of the pp-part is extremely restrictive: in fact, there are no nontrivial étale contractible varieties [HSS14].

3.3 Cancellation questions and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences

We now connect the discussion to the cancellation questions mentioned in the introduction: from the standpoint of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, this can be viewed as a source of many interesting 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences. Before discussing the biregular cancellation problem, we recall some results about the original (birational) Zariski cancellation problem. In the special case where XX is a projective space, this question can be rephrased as follows: if XX is a stably kk-rational variety, then is it kk-rational? The work of Beauville–Colliot-Thélène–Sansuc–Swinnerton-Dyer from the early 80s answered Zariski’s original question in the negative [BCTSSD85], i.e., even over algebraically closed fields, there exist stably rational, non-rational varieties of dimension ≥3\geq 3 (examples over algebraically closed fields cannot exist in dimension ≤2\leq 2 by the classification of non-singular surfaces). The results following this development introduced a heirarchy of birational cancellation questions for discussion of which we refer the interested reader to [CTS07, §1]. Correspondingly, we introduce a heirarchy of “biregular” cancellation questions mimicking the birational story.

Definition 3.3.1.

Suppose XX and YY are irreducible smooth kk-schemes of the same dimension. Say that XX and YY are

  1. 1.

    stably isomorphic if there exist an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that X×𝔸n≅Y×𝔸nX\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\cong Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n};

  2. 2.

    common direct factors if there exists a smooth variety ZZ such that X×Z≅Y×ZX\times Z\cong Y\times Z; and

  3. 3.

    common retracts if there exists a smooth variety ZZ and closed immersions X→ZX\to Z and Y→ZY\to Z admitting retractions.

Remark 3.3.2.

If XX and YY are stably isomorphic, one may ask for the smallest value of mm for which X×𝔸m≅Y×𝔸mX\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m}\cong Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{m}; so it makes sense to refine stable isomorphisms and inquire about mm-stable isomorphisms.

From the standpoint of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, this definition is important because of the following result.

Lemma 3.3.3.

Stably isomorphic smooth varieties are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent.

Perhaps the original cancellation question, which was explicitly stated by Coleman and Enochs [CE71], asked whether 11-stably isomorphic affine varieties are isomorphic. More generally, Abhyanker–Heinzer–Eakin [AHE72] asked whether stably isomorphic affine varieties are isomorphic. In [AHE72], this question is introduced as follows: a ring AA is called invariant if given a ring BB and an isomorphism A⁡[x1,…,xn]≅B⁡[y1,…,yn]A[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\cong B[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}] it follows that A≅BA\cong B. In fact, Abhyankar–Heinzer–Eakin proved that one-dimensional integral domains over a field are invariant [AHE72, Theorem 3.3], i.e., cancellation holds for irreducible affine curves. Then, [AHE72, Question 7.10] asks whether two-dimensional integral domains over a field are invariant, with particular attention drawn to the case of the affine plane. It is, of course, natural to consider the invariance question in higher dimensions as well.

The invariance question becomes more subtle as the dimension of varieties under consideration increases. In the early 1970s, Hochster gave the first counter-example to a cancellation problem over the real numbers [Hoc72], and similar examples were observed by M.P. Murthy (unpublished). In the mid 1970s, Iitaka and Fujita gave geometric conditions (non-negativity of the so-called logarithmic Kodaira dimension, an invariant taking values among −∞-\infty, 00, 11, 22, …\dots) under which affine varieties that are common direct factors are isomorphic [IF77, Theorem 1]. From the point of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, what is more interesting is counter-examples to cancellation questions involving smooth varieties. In the late 80s, Danielewski gave a rather definitive counter-example to the invariance question for smooth affine surfaces: he wrote down smooth affine surfaces depending on a positive integer nn, such that any two varieties in the class were stably isomorphic, and showed that the relevant varieties could be non-isomorphic for different values of nn; we now discuss these varieties in detail.

3.4 Danielewski surfaces and generalizations

Definition 3.4.1.

Fix a polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) in one variable and an integer n≥1n\geq 1. The Danielewski surface Dn,PD_{n,P} is the closed subscheme of 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3} defined by the equation xn​y=P⁡(z)x^{n}y=P(z).

Example 3.4.2.

When n=1n=1 and P⁡(z)=z⁡(1+z)P(z)=z(1+z), the variety Dn,PD_{n,P} is isomorphic to the standard Jouanolou device over ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} from Example 3.1.6. Assuming 22 is invertible in our base ring, it is also isomorphic to the standard hyperbolic quadric x​y+z2=1xy+z^{2}=1.

If P⁡(z)P(z) is a separable polynomial, then it is straightforward to see that Dn,PD_{n,P} is smooth over kk. In that case, projection in the xx-direction determines a morphism Dn,P→𝔸k1D_{n,P}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}. Assume for simplicity kk is an algebraically closed field, so P⁡(z)P(z) factors as a product of distinct linear factors; write z1,…,zdz_{1},\ldots,z_{d} for the d:=d​e​g​P​(z)d:=degP(z) distinct roots of P⁡(z)P(z). In that case, the fibers of the projection morphism are isomorphic to 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} over non-zero points of 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} while the fiber over 00 consists of dd copies of 𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} defined by x=0,z=zix=0,z=z_{i}. The complement of all but d−1d-1 of these copies of the affine line is an open subscheme of Dn,PD_{n,P} that is isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, and the restriction of the projection morphism is a product projection 𝔸k1×𝔸k1→𝔸k1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k}. Thus, the projection morphism Dn,P→𝔸k1D_{n,P}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{k} factors through a morphism Dn,P→𝔸P1D_{n,P}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{P}, where 𝔸P1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{P} is a non-separated version of the affine line with a dd-fold origin. Danielewski and Fieseler observed that this product projection makes Dn,P→𝔸P1D_{n,P}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{P} into a torsor under a line bundle (see [Dub05, Proposition 2.6] for various generalizations of this construction). We summarize the Danielewski construction in the following result, which follows from the discussion above and the fact that torsors under line bundles over affine schemes may be trivialized (i.e., are isomorphic to line bundles).

Proposition 3.4.3 (Danielewski, Fieseler, Dubouloz).

Assume kk is algebraically closed and PP is a separable polynomial. If nn and n′n^{\prime} are distinct positive integers, and PP is a separable polynomial over kk, then set:

Dn,P⟵p1Dn,P×𝔸P1Dn′,P⟶p2Dn′,P.D_{n,P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p_{1}}}{{\longleftarrow}}D_{n,P}\times_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{P}}D_{n^{\prime},P}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p_{2}}}{{\longrightarrow}}D_{n^{\prime},P}.

The morphisms pip_{i} make the fiber product into the projection map for a geometric line bundle. In particular, Dn,PD_{n,P} and Dn′,PD_{n^{\prime},P} are common retracts of Dn,P×𝔸P1Dn′,PD_{n,P}\times_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{P}}D_{n^{\prime},P} (retraction given by the zero section). If P=z⁡(1+z)P=z(1+z), then Dn,PD_{n,P} and Dn′,PD_{n^{\prime},P} are furthermore stably isomorphic.

The above observations, coupled with a homotopy colimit argument allow one to describe the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of Dn,PD_{n,P} rather explicitly: it is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to a wedge sum of d−1d-1-copies of ℙk1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{k}. The proposition even gives very explicit 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences for different values of nn and fixed PP. The isomorphism class of the varieties Dn,z⁡(1+z)D_{n,z(1+z)} may be distinguished over the complex numbers by computing their first homology at infinity: explicitly DnD_{n} may be realized as the complement of a divisor in a Hirzebruch surface.

Proposition 3.4.4 (Fieseler).

If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, then for any integer n≥2n\geq 2, H1∞​(Dn,z⁡(1+z))≅ℤ/n​ℤH_{1}^{\infty}(D_{n,z(1+z)})\cong{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}}. In particular, if nn and n′n^{\prime} are distinct integers, Dn,z⁡(1+z)D_{n,z(1+z)} and Dn′,z⁡(1+z)D_{n^{\prime},z(1+z)} are not isomorphic.

Danielewski’s original construction has been expanded in many directions. We refer the reader to [Dub05] and [Dub07] for more details. One even knows that there are pairs of topologically contractible smooth affine varieties giving counter-examples to cancellation [DMJP11]. Cancellation may fail for open subsets of affine space: this was observed for affine spaces of sufficiently large dimension in [Jel09] and for 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3} in [Dub13]. Jelonek even observed [Jel09, Proposition 3.18] that there exist smooth affine varieties that are 22-stably isomorphic but not stably isomorphic. Subsequently, lower-dimensional examples of this phenomena (though which fail to be smooth) were constructed in [AG18] and 22-dimensional smooth counterexamples were constructed in [Dub19]. Furthermore, cancellation may fail rather generically: for every smooth affine variety of dimension d≥7d\geq 7, there exists a smooth affine variety X′X^{\prime} birationally equivalent to XX such that the variety X′×𝔸2X^{\prime}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{2} is not invariant. We refer the reader to [Rus14] for a survey of the state of affairs up to about 2014, though the references above should make it clear that many exciting developments have occurred since that time.

Problem 3.4.5.

Develop tools to distinguish isomorphism classes of smooth schemes having a given unstable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type.

Remark 3.4.6.

In Section 4.4, we will develop some tools to aid in the study of this problem for smooth schemes that are not proper.

3.5 Building quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties

Winkelmann’s example 10 is realized as a quotient of affine space by a free action of a unipotent group (we review this below in Example 3.5.1. In this section, we discuss some examples that significantly expand on this idea and therefore show that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes are abundant in nature.

Unipotent quotients

If the additive group scheme 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} acts scheme-theoretically freely on a smooth scheme XX and a quotient exists as a scheme, then the quotient map is automatically Zariski locally trivial because H1​(−,𝔾a)H^{1}(-,\mathbb{G}_{a}) vanishes on affine schemes (𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a} is an example of a linear algebraic group that is special in the sense of Serre). In that case, the quotient map is automatically an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence by appeal to Lemma 3.1.3.

Example 3.5.1.

Take k=ℤk={\mathbb{Z}}, and suppress it from notation. Let Q4Q_{4} be the smooth affine quadric in 𝔸5{\mathbb{A}}^{5} defined by the equation x1​x3−x2​x4=x5​(1+x5)x_{1}x_{3}-x_{2}x_{4}=x_{5}(1+x_{5}). Let E2E_{2} be the closed subscheme defined by the equation x1=x3=x5+1=0x_{1}=x_{3}=x_{5}+1=0; E2E_{2} is isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. The complement X4:=Q4∖E2X_{4}:=Q_{4}\smallsetminus E_{2} is quasi-affine and not affine; it is Winkelmann’s quasi-affine quotient from the introduction (i.e., Example 10) over Spec⁡ℤ\operatorname{Spec}{\mathbb{Z}}. The variety X4X_{4} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme by appeal to Lemma 3.1.3.

Generalizing these observations, in [AD07], the first author and B. Doran showed that many (pairwise non-isomorphic) strictly quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties could be constructed in this way. In fact, the following result, which is a first step in the direction of Theorem 1.

Theorem 3.5.2 ([AD07, Theorem 1.3]).

Assume kk is a field. For every integer m≥6m\geq 6 and every integer n≥0n\geq 0, there exists a connected nn-dimensional kk-scheme SS and a smooth morphism π:X→S\pi:X\to S of relative dimension mm, whose fibers over kk-points are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible, quasi-affine, not affine, and pairwise non-isomorphic.

By Proposition 2.4.6, it follows that if XX is any 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth kk-scheme, then P​i​c​(X)=P​i​c​(k)Pic(X)=Pic(k). In particular, if P​i​c​(k)Pic(k) is trivial (e.g., if kk is a field or ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}), then every line bundle on XX is trivial. In that case, every torsor under a line bundle on XX is automatically a 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-torsor. It is known that total spaces of 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-torsors over schemes may have non-isomorphic total spaces (e.g., consider the Danielewski varieties above). The following question extends a question posed initially by Kraft [Kra96, §3 Remark 2] in the case X=X4X=X_{4} (since 𝔾a{{\mathbb{G}}_{a}}-torsors on affine schemes are always trivial, the question is only interesting for quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties).

Question 3.5.3.

Suppose XX is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth kk-scheme. Is it possible to have two 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-torsors on XX with non-isomorphic total spaces?

Winkelmann’s example also has interesting consequences for the shape of the generalized Serre question 6. Indeed, one may use it to see that it is possible to have nontrivial vector bundles on 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes that are not affine. This phenomenon is analyzed in great detail [AD08] as a measure of the failure of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariance of the functor assigning to a scheme XX the set of isomorphism classes of rank rr vector bundles on XX (cf. Example 2.4.7). It also shows that the affineness assertion in Question 6 is absolutely essential.

Example 3.5.4.

The variety X4X_{4} above carries a nontrivial rank 22 vector bundle. The variety Q4Q_{4} carries a nontrivial rank 22 vector bundle. The easiest way to see this is to realize Q4Q_{4} as S​p4/(S​p2×S​p2)Sp_{4}/(Sp_{2}\times Sp_{2}), i.e., as the quaternionic projective line ℍ​ℙ1\mathbb{HP}^{1} in the sense of [PW10]. In that case, the map S​p4/S​p2→Q4Sp_{4}/Sp_{2}\to Q_{4} is a nontrivial S​p2Sp_{2}-torsor, and the relevant vector bundle is the associated vector bundle to the standard 22-dimensional representation of this S​p2Sp_{2}-torsor. In fact, the quotient S​p4/S​p2Sp_{4}/Sp_{2} and the variety Q4Q_{4} both have the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of a motivic sphere, and the relevant morphism is the motivic Hopf map sometimes called ν\nu. Since the open immersion j:X4↪Q4j:X_{4}\hookrightarrow Q_{4} has closed complement of codimension 22, the restriction functor j∗j^{*} on the category of vector bundles is fully-faithful. Thus, this rank 22 bundle restricts to a nontrivial rank 22 vector bundle on X4X_{4}. The total space of this rank 22 vector bundle is another 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme which is necessary non-isomorphic to affine space as it is itself quasi-affine!

We have seen above that there are quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth schemes of dimension d≥4d\geq 4. On the other hand, one may see using classification that the only 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme of dimension 11 (say over a perfect field) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. It follows from a general result of Fujita [Fuj82, §2 Theorem 1] that any topologically contractible smooth complex surface is necessarily affine. Thus, the following question remains open.

Question 3.5.5.

If kk is a field, does there exist an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible (resp. topologically contractible) smooth kk-scheme of dimension 33 that is quasi-affine but not affine?

Other quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties

In [AD07], it was asked whether every quasi-affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible variety could be realized as a quotient of an affine space by a free action of a unipotent group, generalizing the situation in topology suggested by Theorem 2. The answer to this question was seen to be no in [ADF17]. For any integer n≥0n\geq 0, write Q2​nQ_{2n} for the smooth affine kk-scheme defined by the equation ∑ixi​yi=z⁡(1+z)\sum_{i}x_{i}y_{i}=z(1+z) in 𝔸2​n+1{\mathbb{A}}^{2n+1} with coordinates (x1,…,xn,y1,…,yn,z)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},z). Then, define EnE_{n} to be the closed subscheme of Q2​nQ_{2n} defined by x1=⋯=xn=1+z=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{n}=1+z=0. As in the case n=2n=2, EnE_{n} is isomorphic to affine space of dimension nn. We define a variety

X2​n:=Q2​n∖En.X_{2n}:=Q_{2n}\smallsetminus E_{n}.

For n=0n=0, E0=Spec⁡kE_{0}=\operatorname{Spec}k, and X0X_{0} is Spec⁡k\operatorname{Spec}k as well. For n=1n=1, one can check that X2X_{2} is isomorphic to 𝔸k2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{k}. For n=2n=2, X4X_{4} is Winkelmann’s example studied above. The following example shows that not every 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth scheme may be realized as a quotient of affine space by a free action of the additive group, in contrast to the situation in topology summarized in Theorem 2.

Theorem 3.5.6 ([ADF17, Theorems 3.1.1 and Corollary 3.2.2]).

Suppose n≥0n\geq 0.

  1. 1.

    The variety X2​nX_{2n} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

  2. 2.

    If n≥3n\geq 3, then X2​nX_{2n} is not a quotient of affine space by a free action of a unipotent group.

Proof.

We will sketch the proof of the first statement, which follows by induction starting from the fact that X2≅𝔸2X_{2}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{2} and is thus 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. To set up the induction, we introduce some terminology. Let UnU_{n} be the open subscheme of Q2​nQ_{2n} defined by xn≠0x_{n}\neq 0. Note that UnU_{n} is isomorphic to 𝔸2​n−1×𝔾m{\mathbb{A}}^{2n-1}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} with coordinates x1,…,xn−1,y1,…,yn,zx_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1},y_{1},\ldots,y_{n},z on the 𝔸2​n−1{\mathbb{A}}^{2n-1}-factor and coordinate xnx_{n} on the 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}-factor. The closed complement ZnZ_{n} of UnU_{n}, i.e., the closed subscheme of Q2​nQ_{2n} defined by xn=0x_{n}=0 is isomorphic to Q2​n−2×𝔸1Q_{2n-2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} with coordinate yny_{n} on the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-factor. The point x1=⋯=xn−1=y1=⋯=yn=z=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{n-1}=y_{1}=\cdots=y_{n}=z=0 defines a point 00 on ZnZ_{n}. The normal bundle to ZnZ_{n} is a trivial line bundle, with an explicit trivialization defined by the equation xn=0x_{n}=0. Note that, by construction EnE_{n} is a closed subscheme of ZnZ_{n}, and therefore U2​n⊂X2​nU_{2n}\subset X_{2n} as well. Likewise, the subscheme Zn∖EnZ_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n} is isomorphic to X2​n−2×𝔸1X_{2n-2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}.

The closed subscheme of UnU_{n} defined by setting x1=⋯=xn−1=y1=⋯=yn=z=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{n-1}=y_{1}=\cdots=y_{n}=z=0 is isomorphic to 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} with coordinate xnx_{n}. The inclusion map 𝔾m→Un{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to U_{n} is a monomorphism of presheaves, and splits the projection Un≅𝔸2​n−1×𝔾m→𝔾mU_{n}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{2n-1}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}. In particular, the map Un→𝔾mU_{n}\to{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. Likewise, the closed subscheme of Q2​nQ_{2n} defined by x1=⋯=xn−1=y1=⋯=yn=z=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{n-1}=y_{1}=\cdots=y_{n}=z=0 is isomorphic to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} with coordinate xnx_{n} and we have a pullback diagram of the form

where the top map is given by xn=0x_{n}=0 and thus maps on normal bundles to the horizontal closed immersions have compatible trivializations. Since EnE_{n} is disjoint from this copy of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, it follows that we have a sequence of inclusions of the form:

𝔾m⟶𝔸1⟶X2​n.{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\longrightarrow{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\longrightarrow X_{2n}.

We would like to understand the homotopy cofiber of the composite map, which coincides with the homotopy cofiber of the map Un→XnU_{n}\to X_{n} since the projection map Un→𝔾mU_{n}\to{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence.

The cofiber of a composite fits into a cofiber sequence involving the cofibers of the terms by the “octahedral” axiom in a model category. Since 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible, the homotopy cofiber of the map 𝔸1→X2​n{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to X_{2n} is X2​nX_{2n} pointed by 00. The cofiber of 𝔾m→𝔸1{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1} is ℙ1{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}} by the purity isomorphism (see Theorem 2.4.14). Likewise, the cofiber of the map 𝔾m→X2​n{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}\to X_{2n} coincides with T​h​(ν(Zn∖En)/X2​n)=ℙ1+∧(X2​n−2×𝔸1)Th(\nu_{(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n})/X_{2n}})={{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}_{+}\wedge(X_{2n-2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}), and there is thus a cofiber sequence of the form

ℙ1⟶ℙ1∧(Zn∖En)+⟶X2​n.{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\longrightarrow{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\wedge(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n})_{+}\longrightarrow X_{2n}.

By construction, and functoriality of the purity isomorphism (again Theorem 2.4.14), the left hand map is the ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspension of the map Sk0→(Zn∖En)+S^{0}_{k}\to(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n})_{+} given by inclusion of 00 in the first factor. It is therefore split by the map (Zn∖En)+→Sk0(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n})_{+}\to S^{0}_{k} that corresponds to adding a disjoint base-point to the structure map. Thus, one concludes that there is an induced 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence ℙ1∧(Zn∖En)→X2​n{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\wedge(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n})\to X_{2n}. Since (Zn∖En)≅X2​n−2×𝔸1(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n})\cong X_{2n-2}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, it is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible, and the suspension ℙ1∧(Zn∖En){\mathbb{P}}^{1}\wedge(Z_{n}\smallsetminus E_{n}) is also 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. ∎

Question 3.5.7.

Is the total space of a Jouanolou device over X2​nX_{2n} isomorphic to an affine space?

4 Further computations in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory

In the preceding section, we revisited some constructions from affine (and quasi-affine) varieties from the standpoint of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory. Of these, constructions and results, only Theorem 3.5.6 really required tools of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory. To connect with some of the other questions mentioned in the introduction, in particular the generalized van de Ven Question 8, in this section we will discuss connectivity from the standpoint of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, and close with some of the basic computations of the analogs of classical (unstable) homotopy groups of spheres.

4.1 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy sheaves

Suppose (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x) is a pointed space. Earlier, we defined bi-graded motivic spheres Si,jS^{i,j}. These bi-graded motivic spheres allow us to define corresponding homotopy groups.

Basic definitions

Definition 4.1.1.

Given a space 𝒳\mathscr{X}, the sheaf of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected components, denoted 𝝅0𝔸1​(𝒳)\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathscr{X}}), is the Nisnevich sheaf on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} associated with the presheaf U↦[U,𝒳]𝔸1U\mapsto[U,\mathscr{X}]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}.

Definition 4.1.2.

If 𝒳\mathscr{X} is a motivic space, then 𝒳\mathscr{X} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected if the canonical morphism 𝝅0𝔸1​(𝒳)→Spec⁡k\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathscr{X}})\to\operatorname{Spec}k is an isomorphism (and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-disconnected otherwise).

Definition 4.1.3.

Given a pointed space (𝒳,x)(\mathscr{X},x), the ii-th 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy sheaf, denoted 𝝅i𝔸1​(𝒳,x)\bm{\pi}_{i}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(\mathscr{X},x), is the Nisnevich sheaf on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} associated with the presheaf U↦[Si∧U+,(𝒳,x)]𝔸1U\mapsto[S^{i}\wedge U_{+},(\mathscr{X},x)]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}.

As in classical topology, one can formally show that 𝝅1𝔸1​(𝒳,x)\bm{\pi}_{1}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(\mathscr{X},x) is a Nisnevich sheaf of groups, and 𝝅i𝔸1​(𝒳,x)\bm{\pi}_{i}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathcal{X}},x) is a Nisnevich sheaf of abelian groups for i>1i>1. In fact, results of Morel show that, just like in topology, these sheaves of groups are “discrete” in an appropriate sense; see [Mor06] for an introduction to these ideas and [Mor12] for details. The following result, called the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-Whitehead theorem for its formal similarity to the ordinary Whitehead theorem for CW complexes, is a formal consequence of the definitions.

Proposition 4.1.4 ([MV99, §3 Proposition 2.14]).

A morphism f:𝒳→𝒴f:\mathscr{X}\to\mathscr{Y} of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected spaces is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence if and only if for any choice of base-point xx for 𝒳\mathcal{X}, setting y=f⁡(x)y=f(x) the induced morphism

𝝅i𝔸1​(𝒳,x)⟶𝝅i𝔸1​(𝒴,y)\bm{\pi}_{i}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(\mathscr{X},x)\longrightarrow\bm{\pi}_{i}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathscr{Y}},y)

is an isomorphism.

The following result is called the unstable 00-connectivity theorem.

Theorem 4.1.5 ([MV99, §2 Corollary 3.22]).

If 𝒳\mathscr{X} is a space, then the canonical map 𝒳→𝛑0𝔸1​(𝒳)\mathscr{X}\to\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(\mathscr{X}) is an epimorphism after Nisnevich sheafification.

𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid varieties embed into ℋ⁡(k)\mathscr{H}({k})

One rather fundamental difference between the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category and the classical homotopy category is that while classical homotopy types are essentially discrete, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy types may vary in families. We begin by recalling the following definition, which begins to analyze the interaction with morphisms from the affine line and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected components.

Definition 4.1.6.

A smooth scheme of finite type X∈SmkX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid if the map

(4.1.1) Smk​(Y×𝔸1,X)⟶Smk​(Y,X)\mathrm{Sm}_{k}(Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1},X)\longrightarrow\mathrm{Sm}_{k}(Y,X)

induced by the 00-section Spec⁡k→𝔸1\operatorname{Spec}k\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1} is a bijection for every Y∈SmkY\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k}.

Remark 4.1.7.

Let π:Y×𝔸1→𝔸1\pi\colon Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1} denote the projection map. Then the composite map

(4.1.2) Smk​(Y,X)​→π∗​Smk​(Y×𝔸1,X)⟶Smk​(Y,X)\mathrm{Sm}_{k}(Y,X)\overset{\pi^{\ast}}{\to}\mathrm{Sm}_{k}(Y\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1},X)\longrightarrow\mathrm{Sm}_{k}(Y,X)

is the identity. Thus XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid if and only if π∗\pi^{\ast} is surjective or equivalently (4.1.1) is injective for all Y∈SmkY\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k}.

Lemma 4.1.8.

A smooth scheme of finite type X∈SmkX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-local fibrant if and only if it is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid.

Proof.

Since every object of Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} is local projective fibrant, X∈SmkX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-local fibrant if and only if (4.1.1) is a weak equivalence of simplicial sets. We note that every discrete simplicial set is cofibrant and fibrant. Thus (4.1.1) is a weak equivalence if and only if it is a homotopy equivalence or equivalently a bijection. ∎

Corollary 4.1.9.

The full subcategory of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid schemes in Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} embeds fully faithfully into ℋ⁡(k)\mathscr{H}({k}). Moreover, if XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid, the canonical morphism X→𝛑0𝔸1​(X)X\to\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(X) is an isomorphism of Nisnevich sheaves.

Example 4.1.10.

We note that 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid. To show (4.1.1) is injective for all Y∈SmkY\in\mathrm{Sm}_{k} we may assume Y=Spec⁡RY=\operatorname{Spec}R, where RR is a finitely generated kk-algebra. In fact, if RR is a reduced commutative ring, then the pullback map R×→R​[x]×R^{\times}\to R[x]^{\times} is bijective. More generally, any open subscheme of 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid. Similarly, one may show that if XX is a smooth curve of genus g≥1g\geq 1 and U⊂XU\subset X is an open subscheme, then UU is also 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid.

Example 4.1.11.

The scheme ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1} is not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid because π∗\pi^{\ast} is not surjective when Y=Spec⁡kY=\operatorname{Spec}k (there are of course many non-constant embeddings 𝔸1↪ℙ1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{P}}^{1}). We will explore this example more in Section 4.2.

Example 4.1.12.

Recall that a semi-abelian variety is a smooth connected algebraic group GG obtained as an extension

1⟶T⟶G⟶A⟶11\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow 1

of an abelian variety AA, i.e., a smooth connected proper algebraic group, by a torus TT. For example, AA can be the Jacobian of an algebraic curve of positive genus and TT can be the multiplicative group scheme. For any map ϕ:𝔸1→G\phi\colon{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to G the composite 𝔸1→G→A{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to G\to A is constant. To show this we may assume kk is algebraically closed. Indeed every map ρ:ℙ1→A\rho\colon{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\to A is constant: by Lüroth’s theorem, we are reduced to consider the normalization, i.e., we may assume that ρ\rho is birational onto its image. In that case, the differential d​ρ:Tℙ1→TAd\rho:T_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\to T_{A} is injective being non-zero at the generic point. Now the tangent sheaf TAT_{A} is trivial while Tℙ1≅𝒪ℙ1​(2)T_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\cong\mathscr{O}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(2). However, there is no injective map 𝒪ℙ1​(2)→𝒪ℙ1⊕n\mathscr{O}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(2)\to\mathscr{O}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{\oplus n}, where nn is the dimension of AA.

Returning to ϕ\phi we conclude there exists g∈G⁡(k)g\in G(k) such that ϕ\phi factors through the translate g​T⊂GgT\subset G, and we may view ϕ\phi as a map 𝔸1→(𝔸1∖{0})n{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to({\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0\})^{n} for some n>0n>0. It follows that ff is constant because every map 𝔸1→𝔸1∖{0}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0\} is constant. In fact, the affine line provides a useful geometric characterization of semi-abelian varieties by [Bri17, Proposition 5.4.5]: If GG is a smooth connected algebraic group over a perfect field, then GG is a semi-abelian variety if and only if every map 𝔸1→G{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to G is constant.

Finally, since abelian varieties exist in non-constant families, we see 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy types exist in non-constant families.

Remark 4.1.13.

Over the complex numbers, an algebraic variety XX is called Brody hyperbolic if every holomorphic map ℂ→X{\mathbb{C}}\to X is constant and algebraically hyperbolic (also called Mori hyperbolic) if every algebraic morphism 𝔸1→X{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\to X is constant. It is not hard to show that Mori hyperbolic varieties are 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid in the sense above.

4.2 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness and geometry

Having explored varieties that were discrete from the standpoint of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, we now discuss aspects of connectedness in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory. Recall that a motivic space 𝒳\mathscr{X} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected if the canonical morphism 𝝅0𝔸1​(𝒳)→Spec⁡k\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathscr{X}})\to\operatorname{Spec}k is an isomorphism (and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-disconnected otherwise).

Remark 4.2.1.

Since the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category is constructed by a localization procedure, the sheaf 𝝅0𝔸1​(𝒳)\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathscr{X}}) is rather abstractly defined and hard to “compute” in practice. To give one indication of how 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness interacts with arithmetic, suppose XX is a scheme kk-scheme with kk a field. Since stalks in the Nisnevich topology on Smk\mathrm{Sm}_{k} are henselizations of points on smooth schemes, Theorem 4.1.5 implies that if XX is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth scheme, then X⁡(S)X(S) is non-empty for SS every henselization of a smooth scheme at a point. In particular, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth schemes always have kk-rational points.

One would like to have a more “geometric” interpretation of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness. Of course, any 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible space is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected, by the very definition. For this, we recall how connectedness is studied in topology: a topological space is path connected if any two points can be connected by a map from the unit interval. Replacing the unit interval by the affine line, we could define a notion of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-path connectedness. For flexibility, we will use a slightly more general definition.

Definition 4.2.2.

If XX is a smooth kk-scheme, say that XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connected if for every separable, finitely generated extension K/kK/k, X⁡(K)X(K) is non-empty, and for any pair x,y∈X⁡(K)x,y\in X(K), there exist an integer NN and a sequence x=x0,x1,…,xN=y∈X⁡(K)x=x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}=y\in X(K) together with morphisms f1,…,fN:𝔸K1→Xf_{1},\ldots,f_{N}:{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{K}\to X with the property that fi​(0)=xi−1f_{i}(0)=x_{i-1} and fi​(1)=xif_{i}(1)=x_{i}; loosely speaking: any two points can be connected by the images of a chain of maps from the affine line.

Remark 4.2.3.

Note: KK is not necessarily a finite extension, so this definition is nontrivial even when k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}. Indeed, in that case, we ask, e.g., that ℂ⁡(t){\mathbb{C}}(t)-points, ℂ⁡(t1,t2){\mathbb{C}}(t_{1},t_{2})-points, etc. can all be connected by the images of chains of affine lines.

From the definitions given, it is not clear that either 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness implies 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connectedness or vice versa. In one direction, the problem is that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connectedness only imposes conditions over fields: while fields are examples of stalks in the Nisnevich topology, they do not exhaust all examples of stalks.

Proposition 4.2.4 ([Mor04, Lemma 3.3.6] and [Mor05, Lemma 6.1.3]).

If XX is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connected smooth variety, then XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected.

Idea of proof.

The proof uses the fact that we are working with the Nisnevich topology in a fairly crucial way. To check triviality of all stalks, it suffices to show that 𝝅0𝔸1​(X)​(S)\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(X)(S) is trivial for SS a henselian local scheme. Chain connectedness implies that the sections over the generic point of SS are trivial and also that the sections over the closed point are trivial. We can then try to use a sandwiching argument to establish that sections over SS are also trivial: in practice, this uses the homotopy purity theorem 2.4.14! ∎

Conversely, it is not clear that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness implies 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connectedness. However, one may prove the following result.

Theorem 4.2.5 ([AM11, Theorem 6.2.1]).

If XX is a smooth proper kk-variety, and K/kK/k is any separable finitely generated extension, then 𝛑0𝔸1(X)(K)=X(K)/∼\bm{\pi}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(X)(K)=X(K)/\sim. In particular, if XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connected, then XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected.

Remark 4.2.6.

Another proof of this result has been given in [BHS15].

𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness and rationality properties

The preceding theorem suggests a link between 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness and rationality properties. Indeed, Manin defined the notion of RR-equivalence for rational points on an algebraic variety: if L/kL/k is a finite extension and XX is a smooth kk-scheme, we say two LL-points x0x_{0} and x1x_{1} are directly RR-equivalent if there exists a rational map ℙL1→XL{\mathbb{P}}^{1}_{L}\to X_{L} defined at the points x0x_{0} and x1x_{1}. We say two LL-points are RR-equivalent if they are equivalent for the equivalence relation generated by direct RR-equivalence, and we write X⁡(L)/RX(L)/R for the set of RR-equivalence classes of LL-rational points. One says that a variety X/kX/k is universally RR-trivial if X(L)/R=∗X(L)/R=\ast for every finitely generated separable extension L/kL/k. With that definition, a smooth proper variety XX that is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connected is automatically universally RR-trivial, and Theorem 4.2.5 may be phrased as saying that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth proper varieties are universally RR-trivial. In fact, one may make a slightly stronger version of this statement.

Proposition 4.2.7.

If kk is a field and UU is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth kk-variety that admits a smooth proper compactification XX, then XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected and UU is universally RR-trivial.

Remark 4.2.8.

Of course, the hypothesis of admitting a smooth proper compactification is superfluous if either kk has charateristic 00 or UU has small dimension.

Proof.

The easiest proof of this fact uses a tool that we have not yet introduced called the zeroth 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homology sheaf, which plays a role very similar to singular homology in classical topology, but is rather far from motivic (co)homology mentioned earlier. Since U⊂XU\subset X is open, the map

H0𝔸1​(U)⟶H0𝔸1​(X).\mathrm{H}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(U)\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(X).

is an epimorphism by [Aso13, Proposition 3.8]. On the other hand, since UU is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected, there is an isomorphism H0𝔸1​(U)≅ℤH_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(U)\cong{\mathbb{Z}}. Since XX is proper, one concludes H0𝔸1​(X)≅ℤ\mathrm{H}_{0}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}(X)\cong{\mathbb{Z}} as well. Then, the fact that XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected follows from [Aso13, Theorem 4.15]. To conclude, simply observe that if x0x_{0} and x1x_{1} are LL-points in UU, then x0x_{0} and x1x_{1} are connected by a chain of affine lines over LL in XX. Restricting this chain of affine lines to UU gives the required witness to RR-equivalence. ∎

In light of the van de Ven question mentioned in the introduction, we observe that Proposition 4.2.7 has the following consequence on the rationality of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties.

Corollary 4.2.9.

Assume kk is a field having characteristic 00. If XX is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth kk-scheme then XX is universally RR-trivial.

Remark 4.2.10.

If kk is a field and XX is a smooth proper variety, then any 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth proper variety is separably rationally connected. However, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness has cohomological implications, e.g., the (prime to the characteristic part of the) Brauer group of an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected smooth proper kk-scheme is automatically trivial (see [Aso13, §4] for a detailed discussion of this point). For example, it is known that there exist kk-unirational varieties that are not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected [AM11, §2.3] [Aso13, Example 4.18]. Thus, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness of a smooth scheme has nontrivial implications for the rationality properties of the scheme.

We know that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness implies universal RR-triviality for smooth schemes admitting a smooth proper compactification. However, the example of 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} shows that RR-equivalent kk-points need not be connected by (chains of) rational curves. Nevertheless, the following question remains open:

Question 4.2.11.

Is it true for an arbitrary smooth kk-scheme XX that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness is equivalent to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connectedness?

Counterexample in [BHS15]?

Remark 4.2.12.

The relationship between RR-equivalence and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence of points has been studied on certain linear group schemes in [BS15].

4.3 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy sheaves spheres and Brouwer degree

Earlier, we saw that 𝔸n∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0 was a motivic sphere: it was isomorphic in ℋ⁡(k)\mathscr{H}({k}) to Sn−1,nS^{n-1,n}. It is not hard to show that 𝔸n∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0 is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected for n≥2n\geq 2, so it is natural to inquire about its connectivity and to compute its first non-vanishing 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy sheaf. We quickly summarize some results of F. Morel, though we do not have enough space to motivate the proofs.

Theorem 4.3.1 (F. Morel).

If kk is a field, then 𝔸n∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0 is at least (n−2)(n-2)-𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected, i.e., if n≥2n\geq 2, it is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected and 𝛑i𝔸1​(𝔸n∖0,x)\bm{\pi}_{i}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0,x) vanishes for any choice of kk-point x∈𝔸n∖0​(k)x\in{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0(k) and any integer 1≤i≤n−21\leq i\leq n-2.

Morel also computed the first non-vanishing 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy sheaf in terms of Milnor–Witt K-theory introduced earlier.

Theorem 4.3.2 (F. Morel).

If kk is a field, then for any integer n≥2n\geq 2, and any finitely generated separable extension L/kL/k

𝝅n−1𝔸1​(𝔸n∖0)​(L)=𝐊nM​W​(L).\bm{\pi}_{n-1}^{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0)(L)={{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{n}(L).

From this result, Morel deduced the computation of the homotopy endomorphisms of 𝔸n∖0{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0. If k↪ℂk\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}, then 𝔸n​(ℂ){\mathbb{A}}^{n}({\mathbb{C}}) is homotopy equivalent to S2​n−1S^{2n-1}. Therefore, realization defines a homomorphism [𝔸n∖0,𝔸n∖0]𝔸1→[S2​n−1,S2​n−1]≅ℤ[{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0,{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\to[S^{2n-1},S^{2n-1}]\cong{\mathbb{Z}} where the latter identification is the usual Brouwer degree.

Theorem 4.3.3.

If kk is a field, then for any integer n≥2n\geq 2, there is a canonical “motivic Brouwer degree” isomorphism

[𝔸n∖0,𝔸n∖0]𝔸1≅G​W​(k).[{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0,{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0]_{{\mathbb{A}}^{1}}\cong GW(k).

Moreover, if k↪ℂk\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}}, the induced homomorphism G​W​(k)→ℤGW(k)\to{\mathbb{Z}} coincides with the homomorphisms induced by sending a stable isomorphicm class of symmetric bilinear forms to the rank of its underlying ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-vector space.

Later, we will see that computations of motivic Brouwer degree appear in proofs of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility statements.

4.4 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy at infinity

In this section, we introduce some notions of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory at infinity. Unfortunately, we are unable at the moment to make a good definition of “end space” in order to define a workable notion of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-fundamental group at infinity.

One-point compactifications

Fix a field kk, and suppose XX is a smooth kk-scheme. By a smooth compactification of XX we will mean a pair (X¯,ψ)(\bar{X},\psi), where ψ:X→X¯\psi:X\to\bar{X} is an open dense immersion, and X¯\bar{X} is smooth. We will say that such a smooth compactification is good if the closed complement of ψ\psi (viewed as a scheme with the reduced induced structure) is a simple normal crossings divisor.

Lemma 4.4.1.

If XX is a smooth scheme, and X¯0\bar{X}_{0} and X¯1\bar{X}_{1} are smooth compactifications, with boundaries ∂X¯0\partial\bar{X}_{0} and ∂X¯1\partial\bar{X}_{1}, then X¯0/∂X¯0\bar{X}_{0}/\partial\bar{X}_{0} and X¯1/∂X¯1\bar{X}_{1}/\partial\bar{X}_{1} are cdh-locally weak equivalent and thus Σ​X¯0/∂X¯0\Sigma\bar{X}_{0}/\partial\bar{X}_{0} and Σ​X¯1/∂X¯1\Sigma\bar{X}_{1}/\partial\bar{X}_{1} are weakly equivalent in the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category.

Proof.

By definition of the cdh topology, if we are given an abstract blow-up square of the form

i.e., Y→XY\to X is a closed immersion, X′→XX^{\prime}\to X is proper and the induced map X′∖E→X∖YX^{\prime}\smallsetminus E\to X\smallsetminus Y is an isomorphism, then there is a cdh local weak equivalence X′/E→X/YX^{\prime}/E\to X/Y. To establish the statement, simply take the closure X¯\bar{X} of the image of the diagonal map X→X¯0×X¯1X\to\bar{X}_{0}\times\bar{X}_{1} and observe that X¯→X¯0\bar{X}\to\bar{X}_{0} and X¯→X¯1\bar{X}\to\bar{X}_{1} yield abstract blow-up squares. The second statement follows from the first because any morphism of presheaves that is a cdh local weak equivalence becomes a Nisnevich local weak equivalence after a single suspension (i.e., Theorem 2.4.16). ∎

The lemma above shows that one-point compactifications are well-behaved in the cdh-local version of the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category. Alternatively, the S1S^{1}-stable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type of a one-point compactification is well-defined.

Definition 4.4.2.

If XX is a smooth kk-scheme, then for any compactification X¯\bar{X} of XX, we set X˙=X¯/∂X¯\dot{X}=\bar{X}/\partial\bar{X}; there is a natural map X→X˙X\to\dot{X}.

Lemma 4.4.3.

Suppose XX is a smooth scheme. The following statements hold.

  1. 1.

    If XX is proper, then X˙=X+\dot{X}=X_{+}.

  2. 2.

    For any integer n≥0n\geq 0, there is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence (X×𝔸n)˙≅X˙∧ℙ1∧n\dot{(X\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n})}\cong\dot{X}{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}.

Proof.

The first statement is immediate from X/∅=X+X/{\emptyset}=X_{+}. For the second statement, one can first observe that ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n} is a compactification of 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} with boundary ℙn−1{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1} and use the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence ℙn/ℙn−1≅ℙ1∧n{\mathbb{P}}^{n}/{\mathbb{P}}^{n-1}\cong{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}^{{\scriptstyle{\wedge}\,}n}. Then, use the fact that if X¯\bar{X} is any compactification of XX, then X¯×ℙn\bar{X}\times{\mathbb{P}}^{n} is a compactification of X×𝔸nX\times{\mathbb{A}}^{n}. ∎

Stable end spaces

Our goal is to make some progress toward a definition of end-spaces in algebraic geometry. There are many possible approaches to such a definition, and we do not know whether they are all equivalent. One approach is to consider a “punctured formal neighborhood” of the boundary in a compactification; this approach is not suited to motivic homotopy theory using smooth schemes. The following definition is motivated by the definition of singular homology at infinity, in the case where the boundary is suitably “tame”.

J. Wildeshaus introduced the notion of “boundary motive” [Wil06] of a variety; it can be thought of as a motivic version of the singular chain complex at infinity. In fact, with notational modifications, Wildeshaus’ definition gives a ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-stable homotopy type. The only novelty of the definition we give below is that it gives an S1S^{1}-stable homotopy type.

Definition 4.4.4.

Assume XX is a smooth kk-scheme. The S1S^{1}-stable end space is defined to fit into the following exact triangle:

X​∐{∞}⟶X˙⟶e⁡(X)​[1]X\coprod\{\infty\}\longrightarrow\dot{X}\longrightarrow e(X)[1]
Remark 4.4.5.

The main benefit of working S1S^{1}-stably instead of ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-stably is that one has some hope of uncovering unstable phenomena related to “𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected components at ∞\infty”. Indeed, the zeroth 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homology sheaf of a smooth proper scheme (see the proof of Proposition 4.2.7) detects rational points, while the corresponding ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-stable object only sees zero cycles of degree 11 [Aso13, AH11]. Thus, the above definition should be refined enough to detect some algebro-geometric analog of the number of ends of a space.

Proposition 4.4.6.

Assume kk is a field having characteristic 00.

  1. 1.

    The construction e⁡(−)e(-) is a functor on the category of smooth schemes and proper maps.

  2. 2.

    If XX is S1S^{1}-stably 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible, then e⁡(X)≅X˙/∞​[−1]e(X)\cong\dot{X}/\infty[-1].

Example 4.4.7.

The end space of ℝ{\mathbb{R}} is S0S^{0}. Analogously, e⁡(𝔸1)=𝔾me({\mathbb{A}}^{1})={{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}. In particular, end spaces need not even be 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connected. Similarly, we find e⁡(𝔸n)≅𝔸n∖0e({\mathbb{A}}^{n})\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0.

Example 4.4.8.

Suppose XX is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth affine scheme of dimension nn. If XX is isomorphic to 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} then e⁡(X)≅𝔸n∖0e(X)\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus 0.

End spaces as defined here are also compatible with realization. Indeed, the triangle defining e⁡(X)e(X) makes sense in the usual stable homotopy category, and we define eℂ​(X)e_{{\mathbb{C}}}(X) to be the cofiber of the natural map from the suspension spectrum of X⁡(ℂ)​∐{∞}X({\mathbb{C}})\coprod\{\infty\} to the suspension spectrum of X⁡(ℂ)˙\dot{X({\mathbb{C}})}. Because realization behaves well with respect to homotopy cofibers, the following result is immediate.

Proposition 4.4.9.

If ι:k↪ℂ\iota:k\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{C}} is an embedding, then ℜι​(e⁡(X))=eℂ​(X){\mathfrak{R}}_{\iota}(e(X))=e_{{\mathbb{C}}}(X).

Question 4.4.10.

Is there a “good” unstable definition of end spaces in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory?

5 Cancellation questions and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility

5.1 The biregular cancellation problem

After the work of Iitaka–Fujita and Danielewski, it became clear that cancellation questions could admit negative solutions for smooth affine varieties of negative logarithmic Kodaira dimension. Perhaps the main remaining question in this direction is as follows.

Question 5.1.1 (Biregular cancellation).

If XX is a smooth scheme of dimension dd such that

  1. 1.

    XX is stably isomorphic to 𝔸d{\mathbb{A}}^{d}, or

  2. 2.

    XX is a direct factor of 𝔸N{\mathbb{A}}^{N} for some N>dN>d, or

  3. 3.

    XX is a retract of 𝔸N{\mathbb{A}}^{N} for some N>dN>d, or

is XX necessarily isomorphic to affine space?

Remark 5.1.2.

The question of whether varieties that are stably isomorphic to affine space are necessarily isomorphic to affine space is sometimes called the Zariski cancellation question, but as mentioned earlier, Zariski never explicitly stated this question. On the other hand Beilinson apparently asked whether any retract of affine space is isomorphic to affine space [Zaĭ99, §8].

The biregular cancellation question is known to have a positive answer for smooth affine schemes of dimension 11 by [AHE72], and also for smooth affine schemes of dimension 22: the result was established by Miyanish–Sugie and Fujita [MS80, Fuj79] over characteristic 00 fields and extended to perfect fields of arbitrary characteristic in [Rus81]. In contrast, we now know that the biregular cancellation problem admits a negative answer over algebraically closed fields having positive characteristic. Indeed, N. Gupta constructed a counter-example in dimension 33 [Gup14a] and extended this result in a number of directions [Gup14c, Gup14b]. We refer the reader to [Gup15] for more discussion of these results. However, the specific form of these counterexamples does not allow them to be lifted to characteristic 00.

Lemma 5.1.3.

If XX is a smooth scheme of dimension dd that is a retract of 𝔸N{\mathbb{A}}^{N}, then XX is a smooth affine, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible scheme. In particular, any counter-example to the biregular cancellation problem is necessarily a smooth affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible scheme.

Proof.

Any retract of an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence. ∎

Remark 5.1.4.

Gupta’s counterexamples to cancellation above provided the first examples of smooth affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible schemes in positive characteristic.

Remark 5.1.5.

Over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, the biregular cancellation question remains open in dimensions ≥3\geq 3.

Granted the Quillen–Suslin theorem on triviality of vector bundles on affine space, it is easy to see that any algebraic vector bundle on a variety that is a retract of affine space is automatically trivial. The representability theorem for vector bundles guarantees that the same statement holds for 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth affine varieties.

Theorem 5.1.6.

If XX is a smooth affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible variety, then all vector bundles on XX are trivial.

5.2 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility vs topological contractibility

We now compare 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility and topological contractibility in more detail. In particular, we would like to know whether topological contractibility and 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility are actually different. The best we can do at the moment is to proceed dimension by dimension. The only topologically contractible smooth curve is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}. However, already in dimension 22 problems appear to arise.

Affine lines on topologically contractible surfaces

With the exception of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, most topologically contractible surfaces appear to have very few affine lines, as we now explain. Based on the classification results (see [Zaĭ99] and the references therein for more details), it suffices to treat the case of surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimensions 11 and 22 (there are no contractible surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 00).

Remark 5.2.1.

General conjectures in algebraic geometry and arithmetic of Green–Griffiths and Lang suggest that smooth proper varieties of general type should not have “many” rational curves (see, e.g., [Dem12]). Analogously, one hopes that affine varieties of log general type should not have “many” morphisms from the affine line (see, e.g., [LZ17]). The topologically contractible surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 22 contain no contractible curves by work of Zaidenberg [Zaĭ87, Zaĭ91] and Miyanishi-Tsunoda [MT92]; what can one say about morphisms from the affine line to such a surface? For example, are such surfaces Mori hyperbolic (see Remark 4.1.13)?

Remark 5.2.2.

The surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 11 are all obtained from some special surfaces (the so-called tom Dieck-Petrie surfaces) by repeated application of a procedure called an affine modification (an affine variant of a blow-up). How does 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connectedness behave with respect to affine modifications (we understand well how 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connectedness behaves with respect to blow-ups of projective schemes with smooth centers). One could also try to use the rationality results of Gurjar-Shastri, i.e., that any smooth compactification of a topologically contractible surface is rational [GS89a, GS89b].

Based on these observations, it seems reasonable to expect that topologically contractible surfaces that are not isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} are disconnected from the standpoint of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory, which leads to the following conjecture, which suggests an answer to Question 12 from the introduction.

Conjecture 5.2.3.

A smooth topologically contractible surface XX is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible if and only if it is isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}.

The generalized van de Ven Question 8 asks whether all topologically contractible varieties are rational. For 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties, by “soft” methods, one can establish “near rationality” as we observed above. The upshot of this discussion is that 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility is a significantly stronger restriction on a space than topological contractibility. In support of the above conjecture, the following classification result was observed in [DPØ18].

Proposition 5.2.4.

An 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible and 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-chain connected smooth affine surface over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 00 is isomorphic to the affine plane 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}.

Example 5.2.5 ([DPØ18]).

For coprime integers k>l≥2k>l\geq 2, the smooth tom Dieck-Petrie surface is defined as

(5.2.1) 𝒱k,l:={(x​z+1)k−(y​z+1)l−zz=0}⊂𝔸3\mathcal{V}_{k,l}:=\big\{\frac{(xz+1)^{k}-(yz+1)^{l}-z}{z}=0\big\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{3}

We note that 𝒱k,l\mathcal{V}_{k,l} is topologically contractible and stably 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible. However, 𝒱k,l\mathcal{V}_{k,l} has logarithmic Kodaira dimension κ¯​(𝒱k,l)=1\overline{\kappa}(\mathcal{V}_{k,l})=1, and thus it cannot be 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-chain connected. This example shows that the affine modification construction does not preserve 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-chain connectedness. It is an open question whether or not 𝒱k,l\mathcal{V}_{k,l} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible.

Establishing 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-connectedness is a first step towards understanding 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy type. A first step toward answering Question 8 in higher dimensions thus seems to begin with an analysis of the following problem.

Problem 5.2.6.

Which classes of topologically contractible varieties are known to be 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connected?

Chow groups and vector bundles on topologically contractible surfaces

The only general result about vector bundles smooth topologically contractible varieties of arbitrary dimension pertains to the Picard group.

Theorem 5.2.7 ([Gur80, Theorem 1]).

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex variety, then P​i​c​(X)=0Pic(X)=0.

Proof.

Gurjar states this result for affine varieties. To remove the affineness assumption, one may either inspect the proof and see that the assumption is never used, or one may reduce to the affine case by simply observing that P​i​c​(X)Pic(X) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-invariant by Proposition 2.4.6, and any topologically contractible smooth complex variety is is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to a topologically contractible smooth affine scheme by appeal to Lemma 3.1.4. ∎

On the other hand, Theorem  2.4.8 together with standard techniques of obstruction theory allows one to understand vector bundles on topologically contractible smooth affine varieties. Indeed, the ideas of [AF14, AF15] show that classification of vector bundles on smooth affine schemes of low dimensions are reduced to analysis of Chow groups. If XX is a topologically contractible smooth affine complex variety of dimension dd, then one may relate the structure of C​Hd​(X)CH^{d}(X) to geometry. Indeed, if YY is any smooth complex affine variety of dimension dd, then a theorem of Roitman implies that C​Hd​(Y)CH^{d}(Y) is uniquely divisible. Thus, if C​Hd​(Y)CH^{d}(Y) is furthermore finitely generated, it must be trivial. The latter condition may be guaranteed by imposing conditions on the geometry of compactifications and is thus related to the generalized van de Ven question 8. The Chow groups of topologically contractible surfaces, which were originally computed by Gurjar and Shastri [GS89a, GS89b], may be computed in this way. Indeed, Gurjar and Shastri show that the generalized van de Ven question has a positive answer in dimension 22, so it follows immediately that if XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine surface, then C​H2​(X)CH^{2}(X) is trivial.

Theorem 5.2.8.

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex surface, then every algebraic vector bundle on XX is trivial.

Proof.

Suppose XX is a smooth affine surface over an algebraically closed field. By Serre’s splitting theorem, it suffices to prove that rank 11 and rank 22 bundles are trivial. However, P​i​c​(X)≅C​H1​(X)Pic(X)\cong CH^{1}(X). The results of [AF14, Theorem 1] imply that the canonical map

(c1,c2):𝒱2​(X)⟶C​H1​(X)×C​H2​(X)(c_{1},c_{2}):\mathscr{V}_{2}(X)\longrightarrow CH^{1}(X)\times CH^{2}(X)

is a bijection. If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}} and XX is furthermore topologically contractible, then Theorem 5.2.7 implies that C​H1​(X)=P​i​c​(X)=0CH^{1}(X)=Pic(X)=0. The argument that C​H2​(X)=0CH^{2}(X)=0 is given before the statement. ∎

Remark 5.2.9.

In fact, the results of Gurjar and Shastri give a much more refined result than C​H2​(X)=0CH^{2}(X)=0 for a topologically contractible smooth complex affine variety. In [Aso11], the Voevodsky motive of a topologically contractible smooth complex affine surface is seen to be isomorphic to that of a point. This implies that the Chow groups are universally trivial, i.e., for every finitely generated extension L/ℂL/{\mathbb{C}}, C​H2​(XL)=0CH^{2}(X_{L})=0 as well.

Similarly, the generalized Serre Question 6 in dimension 33 may be reduced to a question that is purely cohomological.

Theorem 5.2.10.

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex threefold, then every algebraic vector bundle on XX is trivial if and only if C​H2​(X)CH^{2}(X) and C​H3​(X)CH^{3}(X) are trivial.

Proof.

As in the proof of Theorem 5.2.8, it suffices to treat the case of ranks 11, 22 and 33 by Serre’s splitting theorem. It is known that the Picard group of any topologically contractible threefold is trivial, so the rank 11 case follows. The results of [AF14, Theorem 1] imply that if, furthermore, C​H2​(X)CH^{2}(X) is trivial, then every rank 22 vector bundle is trivial. Finally, classical results of Mohan Kumar and Murthy imply that there is a unique rank 33 vector bundle with given (c1,c2,c3)(c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}) [KM82]. In particular, if C​H3​(X)CH^{3}(X) is also trivial, it follows that every rank 33 bundle on such an XX is trivial. ∎

Remark 5.2.11.

In [Aso11], it is observed that one may produce threefolds with trivial Chow groups by means of the technique of affine modifications, so one may produce many examples of topologically contractible threefolds satisfying the above hypotheses. Similar observations are used in [HKØ16] to establish triviality of vector bundles on Koras–Russell threefolds (see Section 5.3 and the discussion after Theorem 5.3.7 for more details).

As sketched above, one may use geometry to analyze vector bundles on topologically contractible smooth complex affine threefolds. Indeed, suppose XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine threefold admitting a compactification X¯\bar{X} that is rationally connected. Of course, this is weaker than assuming the generalized van de Ven Question 8 has a positive solution in dimension 33. In that case C​H3​(X¯)=ℤCH^{3}(\bar{X})={\mathbb{Z}} and thus C​H3​(X)CH^{3}(X) is trivial. [TZ14, Theorem 1.3] implies that C​H2​(X¯)CH^{2}(\bar{X}) is generated by classes of rational curves. Using this, and the localization sequence, one can sometimes establish that C​H2​(X)CH^{2}(X) is itself torsion. In that case, [Kum86, Appendix Theorem] due to Srinivas implies that C​H2​(X)CH^{2}(X) is actually trivial. For example, it follows from [Kum86, Corollary 18] that if XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine threefold that admits a finite morphism from 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}, then all vector bundles on XX are trivial.

Remark 5.2.12.

For some comments on the situation in dimension ≥4\geq 4, see Conjecture 5.3.11.

5.3 Cancellation problems and the Russell cubic

We now investigate 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible smooth affine varieties over fields having characteristic 00. For concreteness, it’s useful to focus on one particular case: let 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} be the so-called Russell cubic, i.e., the smooth variety in 𝔸4{\mathbb{A}}^{4} defined by the equation:

x+x2​y+z3+t2=0x+x^{2}y+z^{3}+t^{2}=0

There is a natural 𝔾m{{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}}-action on 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} given by

(5.3.1) 𝔾m×𝒦​ℛ→𝒦​ℛ;(λ,x,y,z,t)↦(λ6​x,λ−6​y,λ2​z,λ3​t).{{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}}\times\mathcal{KR}\to\mathcal{KR};(\lambda,x,y,z,t)\mapsto(\lambda^{6}x,\lambda^{-6}y,\lambda^{2}z,\lambda^{3}t).

With respect to this action we have the 𝔾m{{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}}-invariant variables u:=x​y,v:=y​t2∈𝒪​(𝒦​ℛ)𝔾mu:=xy,v:=yt^{2}\in\mathscr{O}(\mathcal{KR})^{{{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}}}. In fact, the GIT-quotient for (5.3.1) is given by

(5.3.2) π:𝒦​ℛ→𝔸u,v2;(x,y,z,t)↦(u,v).\pi:\mathcal{KR}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{u,v};(x,y,z,t)\mapsto(u,v).

The fiber π−1​(α,β)⊂𝒦​ℛ\pi^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)\subset\mathcal{KR} is described by the equations α=x​y\alpha=xy, β=y​t2\beta=yt^{2}, and

(5.3.3) x+x2​y+z3+t2=0.x+x^{2}y+z^{3}+t^{2}=0.

Multiplying (5.3.3) by yy yields the equation

(5.3.4) α+α2+y​z3+β=0.\alpha+\alpha^{2}+yz^{3}+\beta=0.

Using these equations one checks that there is exactly one closed orbit in each fiber. Thus the set of closed orbits is parameterized by the normal scheme 𝔸u,v2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{u,v} and we conclude the corresponding GIT-quotient is indeed (5.3.2).

Makar-Limanov succeeded in showing that 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is non-isomorphic to 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3} [Mak96] by calculating his eponymous invariant. We recall that the Makar-Limanov invariant of an affine algebraic variety XX is the subring ML⁡(X)\operatorname{ML}(X) of Γ⁡(X,𝒪X)\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_{X}) comprised of regular functions that are invariant under all 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX. Using the bijection between 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions on XX and locally nilpotent derivations ∂\partial on the kk-algebra Γ⁡(X,𝒪X)\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_{X}) one finds that

ML⁡(X)=⋂∂ker⁡(∂).\operatorname{ML}(X)=\bigcap_{\partial}\ker(\partial).

Clearly we have ML⁡(𝔸3)=k\operatorname{ML}(\mathbb{A}^{3})=k and similarly for all affine spaces, while extensive calculations reveal that ML⁡(𝒦​ℛ)=k⁡[x]\operatorname{ML}(\mathcal{KR})=k[x]. That is, 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} admits in a sense fewer 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-actions than 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}. Here we observe the inclusion ML⁡(𝒦​ℛ)⊂k⁡[x]\operatorname{ML}(\mathcal{KR})\subset k[x]: the locally nilpotent derivations x2∂z−2z∂yx^{2}\partial_{z}-2z\partial_{y} and x2∂t−3t2∂yx^{2}\partial_{t}-3t^{2}\partial_{y} of k⁡[x,y,z,t]k[x,y,z,t] induce locally nilpotent derivations on the coordinate ring k⁡[𝒦​ℛ]k[\mathcal{KR}]. One easy checks that their kernels intersect in k⁡[x]k[x]. The interesting part of Makar-Limanov’s calculation is to show that ∂(x)=0\partial(x)=0 for every locally nilpotent derivation of k⁡[𝒦​ℛ]k[\mathcal{KR}]. Alternatively one can use Kaliman’s result in [Kal02] saying that if the general fibers of a regular function 𝔸3→𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{3}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1} are isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} then all its fibers are isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. All the closed fibers of the projection map 𝒦​ℛ→𝔸x1\mathcal{KR}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{x} are isomorphic to 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} except for over the origin, which yields a copy of the cylinder on the cuspidal curve {z3+t2=0}\{z^{3}+t^{2}=0\}.

Dubouloz [Dub09] showed that the Makar-Limanov invariant cannot distinguish between the cylinder 𝒦​ℛ×𝔸1\mathcal{KR}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} on the Russell cubic and the affine space 𝔸4{\mathbb{A}}^{4}. Furthermore, M.P. Murthy showed that all vector bundles on 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} are trivial [Mur02] (it is also known that the Chow groups of 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} are trivial). However, the 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}-action on 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} has an isolated fixed point. If 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is not stably isomorphic to 𝔸3{\mathbb{A}}^{3}, is there an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopic obstruction to stable isomorphism?

Question 5.3.1.

Is the Russell cubic 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible?

This question, which has recently been solved in the affirmative, has guided much of the research in the area. First, one might try to compute the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy groups; for this even to be sensible, we should make sure that the first obstruction to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility vanishes. For a generalization of the following observation we refer the reader to [DPØ18].

Proposition 5.3.2 (B. Antieau (unpublished)).

The Russell cubic 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-chain connected.

5.3.3Approach 1.

Can one detect nontriviality of any of the higher 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy groups of 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR}? One approach to this problem is to think “naively” of, e.g., the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-fundamental group. Think of chains of maps from 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1} that start and end at a fixed point up to “naive” homotopy equivalence (this naturally forms a monoid rather than a group). The resulting object maps to the actual 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-fundamental group, but what can one say about its image?

5.3.4Approach 2.

Since to disprove 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractiblity, we only need one cohomology theory that is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-representable that detects nontriviality, it is useful to look at invariants that are not as “universal” as 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy groups. For another approach, using group actions, let us mention that J. Bell showed that rational 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}-equivariant K0K_{0} of 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is actually nontrivial [Bel01]. Unfortunately, his computations together with the Atiyah-Segal completion theorem in equivariant algebraic K-theory also show that the “Borel style” equivariant K0K_{0} is isomorphic to the Borel style equivariant K0K_{0} of a point [AS69]. Nevertheless, 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory gives a wealth of new cohomology theories with which to study the Russell cubic. For example, it would be interesting to know if one of the more “refined” Borel style equivariant theories is refined enough to detect failure of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility.

If μn⊂𝔾m\mu_{n}\subset{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} is a sufficiently “large” subgroup then the μn\mu_{n}-equivariant K0K_{0} of 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is also nontrivial. Moreover, the fixed-point loci for the μn\mu_{n}-actions are all affine spaces (indeed, if nn is prime, then the only nontrivial subgroup is the trivial subgroup which has the total space as fixed point locus). Thus, for many purposes, one might simply look at μn\mu_{n}-equivariant geometry.

In equivariant topology, a map is a “fine” equivariant weak equivalence if it induces a weak equivalence on fixed point loci for all subgroups. Transplanting this to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy theory: if we knew that equivariant algebraic K-theory was representable on an appropriate equivariant 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy category, such a category has been constructed for finite groups by Voevodsky [Del09], and we knew enough about the weak equivalences in the theory, then Bell’s result might formally imply that XX is not 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

The Russell cubic and equivariant K-theory

For representability of equivariant algebraic K-theory let us work relative to a regular Noetherian commutative unital ring kk of finite Krull dimension. We assume that G→kG\to k is a finite constant group scheme (or more generally that it satisfies the resolution property: every coherent GG-module on XX in SchkG\mathrm{Sch}^{G}_{k} is the equivariant quotient of a GG-vector bundle). Under these assumptions, Nisnevich descent for equivariant algebraic KK-theory of smooth schemes over kk was established in [HKØ15]. The fact that equivariant algebraic KK-theory satisfies equivariant Nisnevich descent for smooth schemes implies that it is representable in the equivariant motivic homotopy category.

Let XX be a GG-scheme over kk. Write 𝒫G​(X)\mathcal{P}^{G}(X) for the exact category of GG-vector bundles. Then the equivariant algebraic KK-groups are the homotopy groups KiG​(X):=πi​𝒦​(𝒫G​(X))K_{i}^{G}(X):=\pi_{i}\mathcal{K}(\mathcal{P}^{G}(X)) of the associated KK-theory space, defined by Waldhausen’s S∙S_{\bullet}-construction. We obtain a presheaf of simplicial sets 𝒦G{\mathcal{K}}^{G} on SchkG\mathrm{Sch}^{G}_{k} such that πi​𝒦G​(X)=KiG​(X)\pi_{i}{\mathcal{K}}^{G}(X)=K_{i}^{G}(X) for all XX by applying a rectification procedure to the pseudo-functor X↦𝒫G​(X)X\mapsto{\mathcal{P}}^{G}(X). With the same hypothesis as above, there is a natural isomorphism

KiG​(X)≅[Si∧X+,𝒦G]ℋ∙G​(k)K^{G}_{i}(X)\cong[S^{i}\wedge X_{+},{\mathcal{K}}^{G}]_{\mathscr{H}^{G}_{\bullet}(k)}

for any XX in SmkG\mathrm{Sm}_{k}^{G} and the pointed GG-equivariant motivic homotopy category ℋ∙G​(k)\mathscr{H}^{G}_{\bullet}(k) of kk. This is the desired representability result for equivariant algebraic KK-theory mentioned above.

An explicit computation of the μp\mu_{p}-equivariant Grothendieck groups of Koras–Russell threefolds was carried out in [HKØ16]. For concreteness we specialize to the case k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}. When XX is a complex variety with an action of an algebraic group GG, we let R⁡(G)≃K0G​(k)R(G)\simeq K^{G}_{0}(k) denote the representation ring of GG. If H⊆GH\subseteq G is a closed subgroup, we note there is a restriction map K0G​(X)→K0H​(X)K^{G}_{0}(X)\to K^{H}_{0}(X). Let XX be a smooth affine variety with ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-action and let n>0n>0 be an integer. There is a natural ring isomorphism

(5.3.5) ϕ:K0ℂ×​(X)​⊗R⁡(ℂ×)​R​(μn)→≅K0μn​(X).\phi\colon K^{\mathbb{C}^{\times}}_{0}(X){\underset{R(\mathbb{C}^{\times})}{\otimes}}R(\mu_{n})\xrightarrow{\cong}K^{\mu_{n}}_{0}(X).

An algebraic ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-action on a smooth complex affine variety is called hyperbolic if it has a unique fixed point and the weights of the induced linear action on the tangent space at this fixed point are all non-zero and their product is negative. Recall from [KR97] that a Koras–Russell threefold XX is a smooth hypersurface in 𝔸ℂ4{\mathbb{A}}^{4}_{\mathbb{C}} which is

  1. 1.

    topologically contractible,

  2. 2.

    has a hyperbolic ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-action, and

  3. 3.

    the quotient X//ℂ×X//{\mathbb{C}^{\times}} is isomorphic to the quotient of the linear ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-action on the tangent space at the fixed point (in the sense of GIT).

It is shown in [KR97, Theorem 4.1] that the coordinate ring of a threefold XX satisfying (1)-(3) has the form

(5.3.6) ℂ⁡[X]=ℂ⁡[x,y,z,t]tα2−G⁡(x,yα1,zα3).\mathbb{C}[X]=\frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,t]}{t^{\alpha_{2}}-G(x,y^{\alpha_{1}},z^{\alpha_{3}})}.

Here α1,α2,α3\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3} are pairwise coprime positive integers. We let rr denote the xx-degree of the polynomial G⁡(x,yα1,0)G(x,y^{\alpha_{1}},0) and set ϵX=(r−1)​(α2−1)​(α3−1)\epsilon_{X}=(r-1)(\alpha_{2}-1)(\alpha_{3}-1). A Koras–Russell threefold XX is said to be nontrivial if ϵX≠0\epsilon_{X}\neq 0.

Bell [Bel01] showed that the ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times}-equivariant Grothendieck group of XX is of the form

(5.3.7) K0ℂ×​(X)=R⁡(ℂ×)⊕(R⁡(ℂ×)(f⁡(t)))ρ−1=ℤ⁡[t,t−1]⊕(ℤ⁡[t,t−1](f⁡(t)))ρ−1=ℤ⁡[t,t−1]⊕ℤ(α2−1)​(α3−1),\begin{array}[]{lll}K^{\mathbb{C}^{\times}}_{0}(X)&=&{R(\mathbb{C}^{\times})}\oplus\left(\frac{R(\mathbb{C}^{\times})}{(f(t))}\right)^{\rho-1}\\ &=&{\mathbb{Z}}[t,t^{-1}]\oplus\left(\frac{{\mathbb{Z}}[t,t^{-1}]}{(f(t))}\right)^{\rho-1}\\ &=&{\mathbb{Z}}[t,t^{-1}]\oplus{\mathbb{Z}}^{(\alpha_{2}-1)(\alpha_{3}-1)},\end{array}

where

(5.3.8) f⁡(t)=(1−tα2​α3)​(1−t)(1−tα2)​(1−tα3)f(t)=\frac{(1-t^{\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}})(1-t)}{(1-t^{\alpha_{2}})(1-t^{\alpha_{3}})}

is a polynomial of degree (α2−1)​(α3−1)(\alpha_{2}-1)(\alpha_{3}-1) and ρ≥2\rho\geq 2 is the number of irreducible factors of G⁡(x,yα1,0)∈ℂ⁡[x,y]G(x,y^{\alpha_{1}},0)\in\mathbb{C}[x,y]. In particular, K0ℂ×​(X)K^{\mathbb{C}^{\times}}_{0}(X) is nontrivial. A combination of (5.3.5) - (5.3.8) together with explicit calculations reveal that the μp\mu_{p}-equivariant Grothendieck group of XX is trivial for almost all primes pp. This implies that the suggested approach to showing non-𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility of a Koras–Russell threefold via μp\mu_{p}-equivariant Grothendieck groups cannot work.

Theorem 5.3.5.

Let pp be a prime and let n≥1n\geq 1 be an integer. Let μpn\mu_{p^{n}} act on a Koras–Russell threefold XX via the inclusion μpn⊂ℂ×\mu_{p^{n}}\subset\mathbb{C}^{\times}. Then the following hold.

  1. 1.

    The structure map X→Spec⁡(ℂ)X\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}) induces an isomorphism R⁡(μpn)⊕Fpn→≅K0μpn​(X)R(\mu_{p^{n}})\oplus F_{p^{n}}\xrightarrow{\cong}K^{\mu_{p^{n}}}_{0}(X).

  2. 2.

    FpnF_{p^{n}} is a finite abelian group which is nontrivial if and only if XX is nontrivial and p|α2​α3p|\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}.

If the integers pp and α2​α3\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3} are coprime it follows that every μpn\mu_{p^{n}}-equivariant vector bundle on XX is stably trivial, i.e., for any μpn\mu_{p^{n}}-equivariant vector bundle EE on XX, there exist μpn\mu_{p^{n}}-representations F1F_{1} and F2F_{2} such that E⊕F1≃F2E\oplus F_{1}\simeq F_{2}.

Higher Chow groups and stable 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility

Another natural idea is to study the higher Chow groups of Koras–Russell threefolds. Showing triviality of the said groups goes a long way in concluding 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility of 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR}.

Proposition 5.3.6.
