Let XX be a Koras–Russell threefold of the first kind with coordinate ring

ℂ⁡[X]=ℂ⁡[x,y,z,t](a​x+xm​y+zα2+tα3),\mathbb{C}[X]=\frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,t]}{\left(ax+x^{m}y+z^{\alpha_{2}}+t^{\alpha_{3}}\right)},

where m>1m>1 is an integer, a∈ℂ∗a\in{\mathbb{C}}^{*}, and α2,α3≥2\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}\geq 2 are coprime. For YY any smooth complex affine variety, the pullback map C​H∗​(Y)→C​H∗​(X×Y)CH^{\ast}(Y)\to CH^{\ast}(X\times Y) is an isomorphism.

A related calculation shows the same conclusion holds for Koras–Russell threefolds of the second kind. As for the proof of Proposition 5.3.6 a key input is the observation that the ring homomorphism

ℂ→ℂ⁡[u,v]/(ua+vb)\mathbb{C}\to{\mathbb{C}[u,v]}/{(u^{a}+v^{b})}

induces an isomorphism on higher Chow groups for coprime integers a,b≥2a,b\geq 2.

Combined with the isomorphism between higher Chow groups and motivic cohomology, as shown by Voevodsky [Voe02, Corollary 2], we obtain the following.

Theorem 5.3.7.

Let XX be a Koras–Russell threefold of the first or second kind, and let YY be any smooth complex affine variety. Then the pullback map H∗,∗​(Y,ℤ)→H∗,∗​(X×Y,ℤ)H^{*,*}(Y,{\mathbb{Z}})\to H^{*,*}(X\times Y,{\mathbb{Z}}) induced by the projection X×Y→YX\times Y\to Y is an isomorphism of (bigraded) integral motivic cohomology rings.

A consequence of Theorem 5.3.7 is that every vector bundle on XX is trivial. This was originally shown by Murthy [Mur02, Corollary 3.8] by a completely different method.

Theorem 5.3.7 is a key input in the approach to 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility of Koras–Russell threefolds in [HKØ16]. To proceed it is convenient to employ some techniques from stable motivic homotopy theory. In particular, the slice filtration on the stable motivic homotopy category 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) will be put to good use. Recall the objects of 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) are sequences of pointed motivic spaces related by structure maps with respect to (ℙ1,∞)(\mathbb{P}^{1},\infty). We note that 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) is a triangulated category with shift functor E↦E⁡[1]E\mapsto E[1] given by smashing with the topological circle. Denote by Σℙ1∞​(X,x)∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x)\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) the (ℙ1,∞)(\mathbb{P}^{1},\infty)-suspension spectrum of X∈SmℂX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{\mathbb{C}} and a rational point x∈X⁡(ℂ)x\in X(\mathbb{C}). For fixed F∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)F\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}), we say that E∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)E\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) is

  1. 1.

    FF-acyclic if E∧F≃∗E\wedge F\simeq\ast;

  2. 2.

    FF-local if Hom𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)⁡(D,E)=0\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})}(D,E)=0 for every FF-acyclic spectrum DD.

It is clear that the FF-local spectra form a colocalizing subcategory of 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}). Note that if FF is a ring spectrum, then any FF-module EE is FF-local (every map D→ED\to E factors through D∧FD\wedge F and hence it is trivial if DD is FF-acyclic).

Let 𝐌𝐙∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ){\mathbf{MZ}}\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) denote the motivic ring spectrum that represents motivic cohomology, i.e., for every X∈SmℂX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{\mathbb{C}} and integers n,i∈ℤn,i\in{\mathbb{Z}} there is an isomorphism

(5.3.9) Hn,i​(X,ℤ)≃Hom𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)⁡(Σℙ1∞​X+,𝐌𝐙⁡(i)​[n]).H^{n,i}(X,{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+},{\mathbf{MZ}}(i)[n]).

Here, for E∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)E\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}), the Tate twist E⁡(1)E(1) is defined by E⁡(1)=E∧Σℙ1∞​(𝔾m,1)​[−1]E(1)=E\wedge\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(\mathbb{G}_{m},1)[-1]. The Betti realization of 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}} identifies with the classical Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectrum 𝐇𝐙{\mathbf{HZ}} representing singular (co)homology of topological spaces.

Lemma 5.3.8.

For every X∈SmℂX\in\mathrm{Sm}_{\mathbb{C}} and closed point x∈Xx\in X the suspension Σℙ1∞​(X,x)∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x)\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local.

Proof.

Resolution of singularities allows one to show that Σℙ1∞​(X,x)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) is in the smallest thick subcategory of 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) containing Σℙ1∞​Y+\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+} for any smooth projective variety YY. It suffices now to show that Σℙ1∞​Y+\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+} is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local for such YY. Voevodsky’s slice filtration for any E∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)E\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) is a tower of spectra

⋯→fq+1​E→fq​E→fq−1​E→⋯→E,q∈ℤ.\dotsb\to f_{q+1}E\to f_{q}E\to f_{q-1}E\to\dotsb\to E,\quad q\in{\mathbb{Z}}.

Here the qqth slice sq​Es_{q}E of EE is defined by the distinguished triangle

fq+1​E→fq​E→sq​E→fq+1​E​[1].f_{q+1}E\to f_{q}E\to s_{q}E\to f_{q+1}E[1].

Levine [Lev13] has shown that the slice filtration of Σℙ1∞​Y+\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+} for YY any smooth projective variety is complete in the sense that

holimq→∞fq(Σℙ1∞Y+)≃∗.\operatornamewithlimits{holim}_{q\to\infty}f_{q}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+})\simeq\ast.

Equivalently, if we define cq​Ec_{q}E by the distinguished triangle fq​E→E→cq​E→fq​E​[1]f_{q}E\to E\to c_{q}E\to f_{q}E[1], then

Σℙ1∞​Y+≃holimq→∞cq​(Σℙ1∞​Y+).\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}\simeq\operatornamewithlimits{holim}_{q\to\infty}c_{q}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}).

Since the subcategory of 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local spectra is colocalizing, it now suffices to prove that cq​(Σℙ1∞​Y+)c_{q}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}) is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local for every q∈ℤq\in{\mathbb{Z}}. By definition of the slice filtration, we have cq(Σℙ1∞Y+)≃∗c_{q}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+})\simeq\ast for q≤0q\leq 0. Using the distinguished triangles

sq​E→cq​E→cq−1​E→sq​E​[1]s_{q}E\to c_{q}E\to c_{q-1}E\to s_{q}E[1]

and induction on qq, we are reduced to proving the slices sq​(Σℙ1∞​Y+)s_{q}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}) are 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local. In fact, all slices in 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) are 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local: any slice sq​Es_{q}E is a module over the zeroth slice s0​(𝟏)s_{0}({\mathbf{1}}) of the sphere spectrum, and hence it is s0​(𝟏)≃𝐌𝐙s_{0}({\mathbf{1}})\simeq{\mathbf{MZ}}-local. ∎

Theorem 5.3.9.

Let XX be a Koras–Russell threefold of the first or second kind. Then there exists an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that the suspension Σℙ1n​(X,0)\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible.

Proof.

We first reformulate Theorem 5.3.7 as an equivalence in 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}), using its structure of a closed symmetric monoidal category, see §2.5. The structure map X→Spec⁡(ℂ)X\to\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}) induces a morphism in 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})

(5.3.10) 𝐌𝐙≃ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​Spec⁡(ℂ)+,𝐌𝐙)→ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​X+,𝐌𝐙).{\mathbf{MZ}}\simeq{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C})_{+},{\mathbf{MZ}})\to{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+},{\mathbf{MZ}}).

In view of (5.3.9), Theorem 5.3.7 asserts that for every smooth complex affine variety YY and n,i∈ℤn,i\in{\mathbb{Z}}, there is an induced isomorphism

Hom𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)⁡(Σℙ1∞​Y+​(i)​[n],𝐌𝐙)→Hom𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)⁡(Σℙ1∞​Y+​(i)​[n],ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​X+,𝐌𝐙)).\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}(i)[n],{\mathbf{MZ}})\to\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}(i)[n],{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+},{\mathbf{MZ}})).

The objects Σℙ1∞​Y+​(i)​[n]\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}Y_{+}(i)[n] form a family of generators of 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}), because every smooth variety admits an open covering by smooth affine varieties. Thus (5.3.10) and its retraction ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​X+,𝐌𝐙)→𝐌𝐙{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+},{\mathbf{MZ}})\to{\mathbf{MZ}} induced by the base point 0∈X0\in X are isomorphisms. From the distinguished triangle

𝐌𝐙⁡[−1]→ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​(X,0),𝐌𝐙)→ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​X+,𝐌𝐙)→𝐌𝐙,{\mathbf{MZ}}[-1]\to{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\mathbf{MZ}})\to{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}X_{+},{\mathbf{MZ}})\to{\mathbf{MZ}},

we deduce that ℋom(Σℙ1∞(X,0),𝐌𝐙)≃∗{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\mathbf{MZ}})\simeq\ast. By [Rio05, Theorems 1.4 and 2.2] or [RØ08, Theorem 52], Σℙ1∞​(X,0)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0) is strongly dualizable in 𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}), so that

ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​(X,0),𝐌𝐙)≃ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​(X,0),1​ )∧𝐌𝐙.{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\mathbf{MZ}})\simeq{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\rm 1\hskip-1.72218pt\rule{0.43057pt}{6.54443pt}\hskip 0.86108pt})\wedge{\mathbf{MZ}}.

Thus ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​(X,0),1​ ){\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\rm 1\hskip-1.72218pt\rule{0.43057pt}{6.54443pt}\hskip 0.86108pt}) is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-acyclic, and for any E∈𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)E\in\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C}) we obtain

Hom𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)(E,Σℙ1∞(X,0)∧𝐌𝐙)≃Hom𝒮​ℋ​(ℂ)(E∧ℋom(Σℙ1∞(X,0),1 ),𝐌𝐙)≃∗,\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})}(E,\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0)\wedge{\mathbf{MZ}})\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr{SH}(\mathbb{C})}(E\wedge{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\rm 1\hskip-1.72218pt\rule{0.43057pt}{6.54443pt}\hskip 0.86108pt}),{\mathbf{MZ}})\simeq\ast,

since E∧ℋ​o​m​(Σℙ1∞​(X,0),1​ )E\wedge{\mathcal{H}om}(\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0),{\rm 1\hskip-1.72218pt\rule{0.43057pt}{6.54443pt}\hskip 0.86108pt}) is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-acyclic and 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}} is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local (being an 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-module). By the Yoneda lemma, this implies Σℙ1∞​(X,0)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0) is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-acyclic, i.e.,

Σℙ1∞(X,0)∧𝐌𝐙≃∗,\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0)\wedge{\mathbf{MZ}}\simeq\ast,

On the other hand, by Lemma 5.3.8, Σℙ1∞​(X,0)\Sigma^{\infty}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,0) is 𝐌𝐙{\mathbf{MZ}}-local. Owing to Lemma 2.5.1 this completes the proof. ∎

Remark 5.3.10.

In general, 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-weak equivalences do not desuspend. To illustrate this, for simplicity, take k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, and let {p1,…,pn}\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\} and {q1,…,qn}\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}\} be two collections of complex points in 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}, but the argument works much more generally. If n≥1n\geq 1, then 𝔸1∖{p1,…,pn}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-rigid variety in the sense of Definition 4.1.6. In particular, the 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences 𝔸1∖{p1,…,pn}≅𝔸1∖{q1,…,qn}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\}\cong{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{q_{1},\ldots,q_{n}\} are simply isomorphisms of varieties by appeal to Corollary 4.1.9. However, any isomorphism of varieties of this form is induced by an automorphism of the affine line. The automorphism group of the affine line acts 22-transitively, but not nn-transitively for any n≥3n\geq 3. In fact, as soon as n≥3n\geq 3, there is a moduli space of configurations of dimension n−2n-2.

The variety Σℙ1​𝔸1∖{p1,…,pn}\Sigma_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent to 𝔸2∖{x1,…,xn}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\} for any collection of nn ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-points of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}. Indeed, it is not hard to show that the algebraic automorphism group of 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2} acts nn-fold transitively on 𝔸2​(ℂ){\mathbb{A}}^{2}({\mathbb{C}}) for any n≥1n\geq 1, in contrast to the situation for the affine line. Thus, if we choose coordinates x,yx,y on 𝔸2{\mathbb{A}}^{2}, we may move the points x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} to lie on the xx-axis and then cover 𝔸2∖{x1,…,xn}{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\} by 𝔸1∖{p1,…,pn}×𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\}\times{\mathbb{A}}^{1} and 𝔸1×𝔾m{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}} with intersection 𝔸1∖{p1,…,pn}×𝔾m{\mathbb{A}}^{1}\smallsetminus\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\}\times{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}. The required weak equivalence then follows by the same homotopy colimit argument used to prove that 𝔸2∖0≅ℙ1∧𝔾m{\mathbb{A}}^{2}\smallsetminus 0\cong{\mathbb{P}}^{1}\wedge{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}. By increasing the number of points, we see that there are arbitrary dimensional moduli of smooth varieties that become 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weakly equivalent after a single ℙ1{\mathbb{P}}^{1}-suspension.

The discussion above also has implications for topologically contractible smooth complex varieties. The motivic conservativity conjecture (see, e.g., [Hub08, Proposition 3.4] or [Ayo17, Conjecture 2.1‘]) implies the rational Voevodsky motive of a topologically contractible variety is that of a point. In dimension 22, the integral Voevodsky motive of topologically contractible surface is trivial by the results of [Aso11]; it is also observed there that triviality holds for a number of higher dimensional examples. It thus is not inconsistent with known examples to suggest that the integral Voevodsky motive of a topologically contractible smooth complex variety is always that of a point. In conjunction with the proof of Theorem 5.3.9, the following seems reasonable.

Conjecture 5.3.11.

If XX is a topologically contractible smooth complex affine variety, then there exists an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that Σℙ1n​(X,x)\Sigma^{n}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{1}}(X,x) is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible; in fact, n=2n=2 should suffice.

Remark 5.3.12.

The stronger assertion here is obtained by combining the weaker assertion and a conjecture about conservativity of 𝔾m{{\mathbb{G}}_{m}}-stabilization [BY18]. Conjecture 5.3.11 is reminiscent of an open version of the Cannon–Edwards double suspension theorem [Can79, Edw06]. Conjecture 5.3.11 in conjunction with 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-representability of Chow groups (see Theorem  2.4.10) implies that if XX is any topologically contractible smooth complex variety, then C​Hi​(X)=0CH^{i}(X)=0 for every i>0i>0. In conjunction with Theorem 5.2.10, Conjecture 5.3.11 thus implies that the generalized Serre question has a positive answer in dimension 33.

5.4 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility of the Koras–Russell threefold

In what follows we will outline how Theorem 5.3.9 can be used to show the Russell threefold 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible over any base field of characteristic zero. This was carried out by Dubouloz and Fasel in [DF18].

Observe that 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} contains both the affine line 𝔸y1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{y} and the affine plane 𝔸z,t2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{z,t} intersecting transversally in the origin. The idea is now to show that the inclusion 𝔸z,t2→𝒦​ℛ\mathbb{A}^{2}_{z,t}\to\mathcal{KR} is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-equivalence. There is a naturally induced commutative diagram of homotopy cofiber sequences

(5.4.1)

Here the rightmost vertical map is an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-equivalence induced by the inclusion {0}⊂𝔸y1\{0\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y}: This follows since the normal bundle of 𝔸y1\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y} in 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} is trivial, so that by homotopy purity 2.4.14 we obtain 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-equivalences

𝒦ℛ/(𝒦ℛ∖𝔸y1)∼𝔸1(𝔸y1)+∧(ℙ1)∧2∼𝔸1(ℙ1)∧2.\mathcal{KR}/(\mathcal{KR}\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y})\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y})_{+}\wedge(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{\wedge 2}\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{\wedge 2}.

By a general result we are reduced to showing that ii is an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-equivalence. The perhaps most technical argument in the proof consists of showing that 𝒦​ℛ∖𝔸y1\mathcal{KR}\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-weak equivalent to the punctured affine space 𝔸z,t2∖{(0,0)}\mathbb{A}^{2}_{z,t}\smallsetminus\{(0,0)\}. We discuss this part later in this section. As a consequence the leftmost vertical map in (5.4.1) is a self-map of 𝔸z,t2∖{(0,0)}\mathbb{A}^{2}_{z,t}\smallsetminus\{(0,0)\} up to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-equivalence. As a consequence, its 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-homotopy class is determined by its motivic Brouwer degree (see Theorem 4.3.3). The computation of this degree may be turned into a understanding a certain map in sheaf cohomology with coefficients in Milnor-Witt KK-theory.

Lemma 5.4.1.

Let f:𝔸n∖{0}→𝔸n∖{0}f:{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\}\to{\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\} be a morphism in ℋ⁡(k)\mathscr{H}({k}). Then ff is an isomorphism if and only if

f∗:Hn−1​(𝔸n∖{0},𝐊nM​W)→Hn−1​(𝔸n∖{0},𝐊nM​W)f^{*}:H^{n-1}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{n})\to H^{n-1}({\mathbb{A}}^{n}\smallsetminus\{0\},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{n})

is an isomorphism.

According to Lemma 5.4.1 we are reduced to showing that

i∗:H1​(𝒦​ℛ∖𝔸y1,𝐊2M​W)→H1​(𝔸z,t2∖{0},𝐊2M​W)i^{*}:H^{1}(\mathcal{KR}\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{2})\to H^{1}({\mathbb{A}}^{2}_{z,t}\smallsetminus\{0\},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{2})

is an isomorphism. In effect, we consider the commutative diagram

obtained from (5.4.1). One checks readily that ∂′\partial^{\prime} is an isomorphism, so that i∗i^{*} is an isomorphism if and only if ∂\partial is an isomorphism. Since ∂\partial is a 𝐊0M​W​(k){{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{0}(k)-linear map between free 𝐊0M​W​(k){{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{0}(k)-modules of rank one, it suffices to show the following assertion.

Proposition 5.4.2.

The connecting homomorphism ∂:H1​(𝒦​ℛ∖𝔸y1,𝐊2M​W)→H2​((ℙ1)∧2,𝐊2M​W)\partial:H^{1}(\mathcal{KR}\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{2})\to H^{2}(({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge 2},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{2}) is surjective.

Proof.

As the first row in the above diagram is exact, it is sufficient to prove that H2​(𝒦​ℛ,𝐊2M​W)=0H^{2}(\mathcal{KR},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{2})=0. Fasel’s projective bundle theorem [Fas13] implies

Hi​(𝒦​ℛ,𝐊jM​W)≅Hi+n​(𝒦​ℛ+∧(ℙ1)∧n,𝐊j+nM​W)H^{i}(\mathcal{KR},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{j})\cong H^{i+n}(\mathcal{KR}_{+}\wedge({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge n},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{j+n})

for all i,n∈ℕi,n\in{\mathbb{N}} and j∈ℤj\in{\mathbb{Z}}. Theorem 5.3.9 holds more generally over fields of characteristic zero and shows that 𝒦ℛ∧(ℙ1)∧n=∗\mathcal{KR}\wedge({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge n}=* for n≫0n\gg 0. Combined with the homotopy cofiber sequence

(ℙ1)∧n→𝒦​ℛ+∧(ℙ1)∧n→𝒦​ℛ∧(ℙ1)∧n({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge n}\to\mathcal{KR}_{+}\wedge({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge n}\to\mathcal{KR}\wedge({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge n}

we find Hi​(𝒦​ℛ,𝐊jM​W)=Hi+n​((ℙ1)∧n,𝐊j+nM​W)H^{i}(\mathcal{KR},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{j})=H^{i+n}(({\mathbb{P}}^{1})^{\wedge n},{{\mathbf{K}}}^{MW}_{j+n}) for i≥1i\geq 1, and the latter group is trivial. ∎

Dubouloz and Fasel also give an alternate proof of Proposition 5.4.2 by means of explicit symbol calculations [DF18]. Moreover, the proof of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractibility for 𝒦​ℛ\mathcal{KR} works more generally for Koras–Russell threefolds of the first kind. It is unclear whether a similar proof works for Koras–Russell threefolds of the second kind. The main issue at stake for such a threefold XX is whether there exists an 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalence between the complement X∖𝔸y1X\smallsetminus{\mathbb{A}}^{1}_{y} and some punctured affine plane. On the other hand, in light of Theorem 1 from the introduction the proof is robust enough to provide many new examples of affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties of dimension 33.

Theorem 5.4.3 ([DF18, Corollary 1.3]).

Assume kk is a field. For every integer m≥2m\geq 2, there exists a smooth affine morphism π:X→𝔸m−2\pi:X\to{\mathbb{A}}^{m-2} of relative dimension 33 whose fibers are all 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible. Furthermore, fibers of π\pi over kk-points are pairwise non-isomorphic and stably isomorphic.

Question 5.4.4.

Looking further forward: can one characterize affine spaces among affine 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-contractible varieties in a motivic version of the Poincaré conjecture (e.g., by defining some notion of 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-fundamental group at infinity)?

5.5 Koras–Russell fiber bundles

The geometry becomes much more pronounced in the proof showing that 𝒦​ℛ∖𝔸y1\mathcal{KR}\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y} is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-weak equivalent to the punctured affine space 𝔸z,t2∖{(0,0)}\mathbb{A}^{2}_{z,t}\smallsetminus\{(0,0)\}; the salient geometric features of Koras–Russell threefolds of the first kind have been further developed into the context of Koras–Russell fiber bundles introduced in [DPØ18]. In the following we assume kk is an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero.

Definition 5.5.1.

Suppose s⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]s(x)\in k[x] has positive degree and let R⁡(x,y,t)∈k⁡[x,y,t]R(x,y,t)\in k[x,y,t]. Define the closed subscheme 𝒳⁡(s,R)\mathcal{X}(s,R) of 𝔸x1×𝔸3=Spec⁡(k⁡[x]​[y,z,t])\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}\times\mathbb{A}^{3}=\operatorname{Spec}(k[x][y,z,t]) by the equation

{s(x)z=R(x,y,t)}.\{s(x)z=R(x,y,t)\}.

We say that the projection map

(5.5.1) ρ:=prx:𝒳⁡(s,R)→𝔸x1\rho:=\mathrm{pr}_{x}:\mathcal{X}(s,R)\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}

defines a Koras–Russell fiber bundle if

  • (a)

    𝒳⁡(s,R)\mathcal{X}(s,R) is a smooth scheme, and

  • (b)

    For every zero x0x_{0} of s⁡(x)s(x), the zero locus in 𝔸2=Spec⁡(k⁡[y,t])\mathbb{A}^{2}=\operatorname{Spec}(k[y,t]) of the polynomial R⁡(x0,y,t)R(x_{0},y,t) is an integral rational plane curve with a unique place at infinity and at most unibranch singularities.

Remark 5.5.2.

One can show that a Koras–Russell fiber bundle is isomorphic to 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3} if and only if for every zero x0x_{0} of s⁡(x)s(x) the curve {R(x0,y,t)=0}\{R(x_{0},y,t)=0\} is isomorphic to 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}.

For concreteness we discuss two classes of examples of Koras–Russell fiber bundles.

Example 5.5.3.

Deformed Koras–Russell threefolds of the first kind are defined as

(5.5.2) 𝒳(n,αi,p):={xnz=yα1+tα2+xp(x,y,t)},\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p):=\{x^{n}z=y^{\alpha_{1}}+t^{\alpha_{2}}+xp(x,y,t)\},

where n,αi≥2n,\alpha_{i}\geq 2 are integers, α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} are coprime, and p⁡(x,y,t)∈k⁡[x,y,t]p(x,y,t)\in k[x,y,t] satisfies p⁡(0,0,0)∈k∗p(0,0,0)\in k^{\ast}. By [DF18] it is known that 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p) is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible when p⁡(x,y,t)=q⁡(x)∈k⁡[x]p(x,y,t)=q(x)\in k[x] and q⁡(0)∈k∗q(0)\in k^{\ast}. Note that 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p) is smooth according to the Jacobian criterion since p⁡(0,0,0)∈k∗p(0,0,0)\in k^{\ast}. Moreover, the unique singular fiber of the projection map

(5.5.3) prx:𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)→𝔸x1\mathrm{pr}_{x}:\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}

is a cylinder on the cuspidal curve Γα1,α2:={yα1+tα2=0}⊂𝔸2\Gamma_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}:=\{y^{\alpha_{1}}+t^{\alpha_{2}}=0\}\subset\mathbb{A}^{2}, which is 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible

(5.5.4) prx−1(0)=Γα1,α2×𝔸z1∼𝔸1∗.\mathrm{pr}_{x}^{-1}(0)=\Gamma_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}\times\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z}\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}\ast.

Here (5.5.3) is a flat 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-fibration restricting to a trivial 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-bundle over 𝔸x1∖{0}\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}\smallsetminus\{0\} and 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p) is factorial. The 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-homotopy theory of deformed Koras–Russell threefolds of the first kind (5.5.2) is essentially governed by (5.5.3) and (5.5.4).

Example 5.5.4.

For 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, choose distinct linear forms li​(x)=(x−xi)∈k⁡[x]l_{i}(x)=(x-x_{i})\in k[x], ni,αi,βi≥2n_{i},\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}\geq 2, where αi\alpha_{i} and βi\beta_{i} are coprime, and a∈k×a\in k^{\times}. We define 𝒳m​(ni,αi,βi,a)\mathcal{X}_{m}(n_{i},\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},a) or simply 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} by the equation

(5.5.5) 𝒳m=𝒳m(ni,αj,βj,a):={(∏i=1mli(x)ni)z=∑i=1m((∏j≠ilj(x))(yαi+tβi))+a∏i=1mli(x)}.\mathcal{X}_{m}=\mathcal{X}_{m}(n_{i},\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},a):=\big\{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}l_{i}(x)^{n_{i}}\right)z=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\left(\prod_{j\neq i}l_{j}(x)\right)(y^{\alpha_{i}}+t^{\beta_{i}})\right)+a\prod_{i=1}^{m}l_{i}(x)\big\}.

In the case of two degenerate fibers, (5.5.5) takes the form

(5.5.6) 𝒳2={(x−x1)n1(x−x2)n2z=(x−x1)(yα2+tβ2)+(x−x2)(yα1+tβ1)+a(x−x1)(x−x2)}.\mathcal{X}_{2}=\{(x-x_{1})^{n_{1}}(x-x_{2})^{n_{2}}z=(x-x_{1})(y^{\alpha_{2}}+t^{\beta_{2}})+(x-x_{2})(y^{\alpha_{1}}+t^{\beta_{1}})+a(x-x_{1})(x-x_{2})\}.

For all mm the Makar-Limanov invariant of 𝒳m​(ni,αj,βj,a)\mathcal{X}_{m}(n_{i},\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},a) equals k⁡[x]k[x]; hence it is non-isomorphic to 𝔸3\mathbb{A}^{3}. Moreover, the projection map

(5.5.7) prx:𝒳m​(ni,αj,βj,a)→𝔸x1\mathrm{pr}_{x}:\mathcal{X}_{m}(n_{i},\alpha_{j},\beta_{j},a)\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}

defines a trivial 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-bundle over the punctured affine line 𝔸x1∖{x1,…,xm}\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x}\smallsetminus\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}. Its fiber over the closed point xi∈𝔸x1x_{i}\in\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x} is isomorphic to the cylinder on the cuspidal curve Γαi,βi:{yαi+tβi=0}\Gamma_{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i}}:\{y^{\alpha_{i}}+t^{\beta_{i}}=0\}. By counting closed fibers non-isomorphic to 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} one concludes that 𝒳m\mathcal{X}_{m} and 𝒳m′\mathcal{X}_{m^{\prime}} are non-isomorphic when m≠m′m\neq m^{\prime}.

Now we turn to the geometric properties of deformed Koras–Russell threefolds as in Example 5.5.3. In particular, this will explain the 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-equivalence between 𝒦​ℛ∖𝔸y1\mathcal{KR}\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{y} and the punctured affine plane.

There is an induced 𝔾a\mathbb{G}_{a}-action on 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p) determined by the locally nilpotent derivation

∂=xn​∂∂y+(α1​yα1−1+x​∂∂y​p​(x,y,t))​∂∂z,\partial=x^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}+(\alpha_{1}y^{\alpha_{1}-1}+x\frac{\partial}{\partial y}p(x,y,t))\frac{\partial}{\partial z},

on the coordinate ring of 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p), with fixed point locus the affine line {x=y=t=0}≅𝔸z1\{x=y=t=0\}\cong\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z}. The geometric quotient 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)→𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)/𝔾a\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\rightarrow\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)/\mathbb{G}_{a} yields an 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)∖𝔸z1→𝔖⁡(α1,α2)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z}\rightarrow\mathfrak{S}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}) in the category of algebraic spaces [Knu71]. In fact there exists a factorization

(5.5.8)

where π|\pi_{|} is the restriction of π=prx,t:𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)→𝔸x,t2\pi=\text{pr}_{x,t}:\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\rightarrow\mathbb{A}^{2}_{x,t} to 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)∖𝔸z1\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z}. To construct (5.5.8) we form a cyclic Galois cover of 𝔸x,t2\mathbb{A}^{2}_{x,t} of order α1\alpha_{1} and hence of 𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p) by pullback via π\pi. The maps arise as geometric quotients for μα1\mu_{\alpha_{1}}-equivariant maps by gluing copies of 𝔸2∖{(0,0)}\mathbb{A}^{2}\smallsetminus\{(0,0)\} via a family of cuspidal curves. Here ρ\rho is an étale locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundle, we have 𝔖⁡(α1,α2)≅𝔖⁡(α1,1)\mathfrak{S}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\cong\mathfrak{S}(\alpha_{1},1), and both of the projection maps for the smooth quasi-affine 44-fold

(5.5.9) (𝒳⁡(n,αi,p)∖𝔸z1)×𝔖⁡(α1,α2)(𝒳⁡(n,α1,1,p)∖𝔸z1)(\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z})\times_{\mathfrak{S}(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})}(\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{1},1,p)\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z})

are Zariski locally trivial 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-bundles, and hence 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-weak equivalences. The fiber product in (5.5.9) is formed in algebraic spaces over the punctured affine plane 𝔸x,t2∖{(0,0)}\mathbb{A}^{2}_{x,t}\smallsetminus\{(0,0)\}. Furthermore, the projection map prx:𝒳⁡(n,α1,1,p)→𝔸x1\text{pr}_{x}:\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{1},1,p)\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x} is a trivial 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2}-bundle. It follows that 𝒳⁡(n,α1,1,p)≅𝔸x,y,z3\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{1},1,p)\cong\mathbb{A}^{3}_{x,y,z} and we can finally conclude that there exist 𝔸1{\mathbb{A}}^{1}-weak equivalences

𝒳(n,αi,p)∖𝔸z1∼𝔸1𝒳(n,α1,1,p)∖𝔸z1∼𝔸1𝔸x,t2∖{(0,0)}.\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{i},p)\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z}\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}\mathcal{X}(n,\alpha_{1},1,p)\smallsetminus\mathbb{A}^{1}_{z}\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}\mathbb{A}^{2}_{x,t}\smallsetminus\{(0,0)\}.

The currently most general result concerning 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractibility of Koras–Russell fiber bundles was shown in [DPØ18].

Theorem 5.5.5.

Suppose ρ:𝒳⁡(s,R)→𝔸x1\rho:\mathcal{X}(s,R)\to\mathbb{A}^{1}_{x} is a Koras–Russell fiber bundle with basepoint the origin. The S1S^{1}-suspension and hence the ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-suspension of 𝒳⁡(s,R)\mathcal{X}(s,R) are 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{1}-contractible:

𝒳(s,R)∧S1∼𝔸1𝒳(s,R)∧ℙ1∼𝔸1∗.\mathcal{X}(s,R)\wedge S^{1}\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}\mathcal{X}(s,R)\wedge\mathbb{P}^{1}\sim_{\mathbb{A}^{1}}\ast.
Question 5.5.6.

Can one generalize the notion of a Koras–Russell fiber bundle and show Theorem 5.5.5 over arbitrary fields of characteristic zero?

Remark 5.5.7.

Work on Question 5.5.6 is likely to involve base change arguments to an algebraic closure.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
